paragraphs: Attaching i-cord to the edge of a knitted piece adds a nice finishing touch. There are unlimited variations to this technique. Here are three for you to try. The first is plain i-cord along the edge. The second adds a few extra rows in between and is a variation of the worm trim that you may know.

I've heard the third call a helicopter trim. Watch and see why this is a very appropriate name. Begin by casting on three stitches. Designer your machine to slip in one direction. If you aren't familiar with this, look for the Knit It Now video on knitting i-cord.

Pick up one loop of the knitted garment and hang it on the end needle. This could be an edge stitch or a stitch on the caston or bound off edge. Knit across and back, slipping in one direction. Repeat this across the edge of the piece you're finishing.

Try this technique first on your swatch to check the gauge. But I generally use the garment tension to knit an i-cord edge. When you get to a corner, just knit a couple of extra rows without picking up the garment stitch. Keep picking up and knitting.

Picking up and knitting and soon you'll see that you have a beautiful edge that looks great on both sides. The second i-cord edge is done the same way, except you knit a few rows between the pickup. In this example, we're knitting three rows with six passes of the carriage before picking up the next stitch.

Pick up the next stitch or skip a few. Try it both ways again. Try this on a swatch. It tends to flare and may not be appropriate for your project. The helicopter trim is done similarly to the previous edge, but the trim is twisted before you pick up the next stitch.

As before, we're knitting three rows with six passages of the carriage. Then turn the work for a few turns and make sure the private side of the work is facing you again. Then pick up the next stitch of your knitted piece.

Repeat this across the row. Again, you can pick up the next stitch or skip a few rows as you can see. See, the number of turns determines the shape of the twisted i-cord that forms. Mastering i-cord will go a long way in creating your own designs.
Play and have fun with them.

Knit it Now memember recently requested instruction to make finished slashes in the middle of a knitted piece. She wanted to convert a hand knitting pattern that used this technique. First, have a cast on rag or knitted swatch ready.

These need to be large enough to fill the number of needles in the slash they'll be used to make the second half of the slash easier to knit. I'm assuming you know how to put your machine into hold position, so that any needles that are pulled all the way out do not knit.

I'll refer to the right set of stitches. The center set of stitches, which is the opening and the left set of stitches is you see them on the needle bed. Cast on and knit the desired length to the slash put the left and the center needles and to hold position.

With the carriage on the right. Set your machine to hold and knit across the right needles. You'll notice that the yarn is in position to work on the center set of needles. You'll be binding these stitches off using the method of your choice.

This bind off creates the opening for the slash. Once you're done with the bind off, push those center needles to out of work position. Notice that your yarn is now in position to work the left set of needles. But your carriage is on the left, so you need to make a free pass to get it to the right hand side.

Push any needles with stitches into hold position. With the carriage still on hold, make your free pass. Then push the left set of needles into working position and knit to the left across these needles. You'll have completed the first row.

The right set of stitches were knit, the center set were bound off, and the left stitches were knit all in one row. Your row counter should only advance to one. The next row we'll fill in the empty needles to complete the slash.

First hang the cast on rag or the swatch on the center set of needles. This will allow you to hang weights and make the knitting easier. Manually knit one row of Ravel cord. In this image, notice the yellow Ravel cord and the bound off slash behind the purple cast on rag.

Make sure your carriage is still set to hold. Both the center set of needles and the right needles are in hold knit across the left needles. You'll notice now that the yarn is in position to work the center needles. Using the method of your choice cast on those center 20 stitches.

This will finish the opening of the slash. When you're done casting on. You'll notice that your yarn is now in position to knit the right set of stitches, but the carriage is on the right. So put all of the needles in hold for a free pass and position the carriage on the left.

Be sure the left and the center needles are in hold and then knit the right set of stitches. Now set your carriage to knit all the stitches. Remove the hold setting and knit across the row. The slash is complete. You can continue knitting as desired When you remove the Ravel cord and the cast on rag, you'll see your slash.

the pattern she was using called for a number of random slashes and the edges just simply rolled Thank you for watching. The Knit it Now learning library has hundreds of techniques on a variety of subjects at all skill levels.

Have you ever needed to both start and end a knitted piece with a hem? Scarves and blankets are good examples for using this technique. Here is an overview of knitting an item with a reverse hem. You'll start with a normal hem and knit the body of your item.

Towards the end of your knitting, you're going to knit a marker row. We'll talk about a couple different methods of marker rows. You'll knit the public side of the hem. You'll knit a turning row, knit the private side of the hem, and then hang the hem from that marked row and bind off.

One of the simplest marking rows is to simply use a contrasting color sewing thread and knit that in the row that you want to mark. You can use the contrasting color to pick up the hem and remove that sewing thread easily.

When you're done. Try weaving ravel cord over and under every other needle. You can then remove the ravel cord. Also, after you've picked up your hem. Try slipping every other needle for a marker row. For this example, we are adjusting our tension of our hem.

I'm assuming that you've already done the first part of your hem, so just repeat whatever tension changes you did on the first part of your hem on the reversed hem. You'll knit the body of your piece, knit the public side of your hem, knit a turning row, and the private side of your hem.

Now you put that marker row to work. You can pick up every stitch or every other stitch. We just want to get a nice join for the hem. As always in knitting, you've got some choices in binding off this reverse hem. After you hang the marked row, you could use a tapestry needle or a double-eye needle and just run a tail of yarn through the stitches.

This will secure this hem very well. If you do this neatly, the hem lays very, very flat. One suggestion is to knit the last row more tightly to reduce the size of the loops. Another idea is for a really fast finish, is to just bind off those stitches using whatever bindoff method you'd like.

Whatever method you choose, the hems will be beautiful on both edges of your item. Thank you for watching Machine Knitting Now Learning Library has hundreds of techniques on a variety of subjects at all skill levels. Please consider a subscription and let us help you be a better machine knitter.

Getting started to knit quickly is a snap using Garment Designer. How many times have you wanted to make a quick sweater for an upcoming baby shower? You wanted something quick and easy and you wanted to take time to embellish the garment and not spend a whole lot of time in front of the compute.

With Garment Designer you can do this in just a few steps. We're going to create this cardigan simple baby cardigan in less than 10 steps. Let's get started. When you start a new pattern, the first thing you'll notice is that there's a default garment on the screen.

We will use this as our starting point. Also, you'll see lots of lines. The green lines represent the sloper which actually represents the body and the black line is the actual pattern. So we are showing that we have some breathing room, some ease in this garment.

To make things simpler. Let's go ahead and turn the sloper off we'll click >display and >show pattern. And that makes things a whole lot easier to see. Now we're going to be designing a cardigan. Let's set up our pieces >display and >pieces.

Our garment pieces are front. We both need both a right and a left, but they're not going to be joined because it's a cardigan, they will be independent. We need a right and a left back, but we want those joined. We want one single back.

Our Sleeve has a front and a back but we also want it joined. There's no seam down that sleeve. We're only going to work with one sleeve. We don't need both of them on the screen. Click. OK and there we go. Looks like we're getting close here.

Now before we forget let's enter our gauge. We'll go to >options >units and gauge. We've got some choices here. I'm going to use stitches and rows per inch. Five and seven and click, OK. The next thing we need to set up on our pattern is a size.

We're going to be making a child sweater. I don't want to do an infant's let's make it a toddler sweater. So that baby has something to grow into. We can change the size here. We'll make it a 2 toddlers. And one thing I do notice is that this is a set in sleeve now for baby sweaters.

I don't need to be bothered. This is supposed to be quick and easy. Let's make this just a straight drop shoulder sleeve. Again, very little shaping quick and easy. Another thing that I notice is there is a sloped shoulder. For children's clothing you really don't need to slope that shoulder.

It's just a little more shaping while you're knitting. Again we want this thing to be fast. Change it from sloped to straight and there we are. We've got the basics of our sweater. Believe it or not. We're ready to start knitting.

I'd like to save this garment we'll >file and >save as and we'll call it BABY and click on Save. The next thing we want to do is see the pattern. Where are my instructions? I've got some nice pretty pictures on the screen. will click >generate >shaping instructions and voila.

There's our shaping instructions. Click >file and >print these will print out for you. Take them over to your knitting machine and you are ready to go. Very few steps, a couple of minutes and you're ready to go. Now If you're not used to the shaping instructions in Garment Designer they're little bit different, but the first time you use them you will fall in love with them.

You follow the instructions from the bottom up. So this is our right front. We're going to cast on 31 stitches. We're going to knit to row 81. And it row 81 we're going to start shaping our neckline. We're going to take off 2 stitches which will leave us 29.

The next row we're going to be taking off 2 stitches on the right hand side. Take us down to 27 all the way up to Row 90 where our last shaping takes place. Row 95 we're all done and will bind off 21. So the next time you want a really quick sweater.
Turn to Garment Designer and you'll be knitting in no time.

You can control the needle selection for easier seaming. You can enter the pattern width. This is not, may or may not be the knitting with just the stitch pattern width you can position the design on your knitted piece. And you can also select a portion of the stitch pattern to use.

For this example, we're going to center our duck over 25 stitches. We also want the pattern shifted over a bit to be off center on the garment. When we download and preview our duck with these settings, you'll see that the pattern controller followed our instructions perfectly.

We have a margin on the left and our duck is centered over the 25 stitches. Notice that at the bottom of the interactive knitting screen are shown the stitches and rows in our design, as well as the point cam positions. It also includes a contrasting color indicator.

For our next example. We only want to use the flowers at the bottom of this design. We've already opened the bear pattern and we've been downloaded the entire thing one time. We'll use the knit button again to preview the design close up.

And you'll see that we only want those first eight rows row one through eight of the pattern for our new design. Now close the knit screen and we'll click the download button again. On the downloads screen, we will edit the pattern indicators section and tell the Silver Knit utility what rows we want to use.

Click okay. Click knit to preview and you'll see that it's chosen the eight rows of flowers that we want, and these will transfer to our knitting machine. The Silver Knit pattern controller is a great option for silver or a singer.

Now, if you have a replacement sponge bar on hand, now might be a good time to replace it. Get started replacing that needle by pulling out your sponge bar just to the position of the bent or broken needle. Reach the other end and grab the opposite end of the sponge bar to pull it out.

Now notice how the needles pop up when the sponge bar is removed. This will allow you to take out that broken needle. Grab the butt of the needle and pull it towards you. Lifting up on the back of the needle, push it back and up and wiggle it a little bit, and then pull the hook end out of the slot.

Now replace the needle in the reverse order. Place the hook end in the slot. Pull it forward and drop the back of the needle. End of the track and push back. Use your needle pusher to hold down the needles and slide that sponge bar back into place.

Have you ever found a knitting pattern that you love, but the neckline was too high or way too low? Recalculating a round neckline is the next topic in our Pencil and Paper Charting series. If you missed the first three basics tutorials, you'll want to watch them first, we will build on the skills learned.

Let's use this front neckline schematic and make it a little more comfortable. The pattern gauge is 7stitches and 10.5 rows per inch. The armhole is 9 inches deep and the neckline in the original pattern is 4 inches deep. First thing we want to reset our row counter to 000 at the beginning of the armhole shaping.

Now we've decided we want our new neck depth to be 6 inches deep. That means we'll knit 3 inches before we start our shaping. If we do the math, we'll multiply three times our row gauge, do a little rounding and we'll see that on row 32, we start our neckline shaping.

There will be a total of 64 rows in the neckline to complete the piece. Now the fun starts. Let's figure out how to create the curves for our round neck. Let's start with our graph paper method. We'll work with half of the neckline.

Mark off 28 stitches by 64 rows. Remember to use knitting graph paper. Now sketch a nice curve. Quickly draw in some stitches to follow the curve. Now you'll notice that we're decreasing three stitches every other row and then two stitches every other rows, and then three stitches every fourth row.

This is pretty messy, difficult to knit, and hard to duplicate on the other side of the neckline. There's a better way. Here's the classic formula for shaping a neckline. Bind off half the stitches. Decrease the remaining stitches, one stitch every other row, then knit straight until the neckline is completed.

This gives you a pretty nice curve. Remember, this is knitting, and by the time you attach a band, you'll never see that this is a straight line decrease. Finish by writing your pattern. At row 32, bind off the center 28 stitches, working each side separately.

Decrease on the neckline edge, one stitch every other row 14 times knit even to row 96. Even though we did our calculations over half the neckline, it's common practice to bind off all of the center stitches at one time. This creates a nicer center front and makes it easier to finish the neckline.

If this method isn't accurate enough for your taste, there are other formulas you can use to get a more gradual and graceful curve. I recommend the book Knitwear Design Workshop as an excellent resource for designing. Purchasing from this link supports Knit it Now.
Thank you for watching and look for many more tutorials in the extensive Knit It Now Learning Library. Here's a link to all the tutorials in this series. Happy charting.

In this tutorial, we'll discuss upper arm size and set in sleeves. Like ready-made clothing, commercial sweater patterns are created based on a set of standards. What if you aren't standard size? We covered lengthening and shortening sleeves in a previous tutorial.

Let's consider changing the upper arm and the impact on the sleeve head. Imagine how uncomfortable this purple sweater must be to where there's no ease and the knitting is stretched over the model's upper arm. This can often be an issue when it in plus size sweaters and for men's sweaters as well.

The sleeve head indicated by the yellow line must match the armhole opening. In classic dress making the sleeve head has a bit of ease, but for this example, we'll just ignore the ease. Now what happens if you just make the upper arm of the sleeve larger?

The sleeve head is enlarged and it's no longer going to fit in the arm hole. We don't want to alter the depth of the arm hole. We just want to add fullness over the upper arm. Let's picture a paper pattern. We can slash that paper pattern and spread the upper arm to the proper dimension.

Now if we stop here again, the sleeve head's going to be too large. But by dropping down the top of the sleeve head redrawing the shape will accomplish what we need for our sleeve to fit, and the sleeve head will still match the arm hole opening.

One thing to notice is that the cuff size is also enlarged. If you do this, and you may not want that, you can always alter the size of the cuff and recalculate the underarm shaping. Let's continue with the sleeve head. Now let's look at this another way.

We'll take the curves out of the equation for now. The initial bind offs won't change and the final bind offs are not going to change. All we're going to do is reshape the sleeve head in the area shown by the yellow line. Once again, we'll make the upper arm wider.

I'll just rotate that yellow line and it's clear that the sleeve head's going to be too large, so what we need to do is drop that final bind off area. So the length of the yellow line remains the same and the sleeve head will fit into the arm hole.

Here's another thing to notice. Not only is the upper arm of the sleeve wider, but the shape of the sleeve head changes as well on the purple sweater. The model could use more fabric. Across her top of her arm. Changing the shape of the sleeve head would greatly improve the fit of this sweater.

Okay. Now we understand the issues surrounding modifying a set in sleeve. What we've done is fine for a paper sewing pattern. You just redraw a nice curve and you're all set as long as the sleeve had measurement and matches the armhole opening.
Now what about knitting? In our next tutorial, we'll talk about different methods for drafting the sleeve head for knitting.

Have you ever had your knitting fall off the machine, get your carriage stuck, or find that a stitch pattern is just not working? Even the most experienced machine knitter has one of THOSE days, now and then. In this video, we'll cover some of the common things that can happen, and we'll talk about how to avoid them.

A lot of things can go wrong when casting on. I can't cover all the different cast-on methods. Each has their own little quirk, but there are some general things to watch out for. If your carriage jams after you cast on, it might be that the carriage isn't seated correctly on the needle bed.

Remove it and the yarn, replace the carriage, and run it across the needle bed with all the needles out of work. It should move smoothly and easily. Maybe your cast on is too tight. Remove the yarn from the needles and cast on more loosely with the method of your choice, or maybe try a different cast on method.

Check to make sure that you're using the yarn that's the correct size for the needles of your machine. When you're using the right yarn, your carriage will move smoothly and easily and won't jam. Maybe the yarn tension is too tight.

Make sure that it's not caught up in the yarn guides and check maybe the tensioner for tangles and knots. It needs to be loose enough to feed through the carriage so it can move easily. If you've pulled all the needles out maybe to do an E-wrap cast on and they don't knit when you push the carriage across, maybe you have the machine set to hold.

Check your hold setting on your carriage, disable the hold, and try again. Sometimes after casting on all the stitches drop or they make large loops in a big yarn mess. Check to make sure that the yarn is engaged in the yarn feeder of the carriage correctly.

Also, check that it's in the right feeder. Some machines have two yarn feeders. Another thing that can happen is that your sinker plate is not seated properly in the carriage. Remove the carriage, reseat that sinker plate, and try again.

If, after casting on some stitches drop at the beginning of the row, your yarn is probably too loose. Try again and adjust the tensioner and try taking up the slack of the yarn at the beginning of the row. If stitches drop in the middle of the row, probably the sinker plate is not seated properly.

Loosen the screws holding the sinker plate, push them back in, reseed it, take the whole carriage off. Make sure that the sinker plate is attached to the carriage correctly. Another issue could be that yarn is tangled in the sinker brushes.

Remove your carriage, look underneath, make sure there isn't any yarn or lint stuck in those brushes. Now, if the stitches drop in the middle of the row, the cast-on might be too loose or just uneven. Confirm that the stitches of your original cast-on are even.

If you find that stitches are tucking or they just don't knit off the needles properly, your cast on is probably too tight or the stitch tension is way too low. Those stitches are way too tight. You can knit individual stitches manually to fix this or take everything off the machine and try it again.

Sometimes the stitches just won't knit. Maybe your cast on is too loose or your controls are not set to plain knitting. It sounds silly, but take a look and make sure that the settings on your carriage are set for plain knitting.

No matter what's happening, if you're struggling with your cast on, check these things. Are you using the right yarn for your machine? Are the settings on your carriage correct? Is the carriage seated on the needle bed properly?

Are the sinker plate in the carriage joined correctly? Okay. Check your yarn. Is it feeding smoothly without any knot, or tangles, or hangups anywhere? Is your yarn in the right feeder of the carriage? Is your cast on too tight, too loose?

Try this. Try casting on with another method. You might have more success. Sometimes all it takes is getting up, taking a deep breath, walk away, and come back to it, and your problem is solved. Happy knitting.

Have you ever had your knitting fall off the machine? Get your carriage stuck? Or find that a stitch patterns, just not working? Even the most experienced machine has one of those days now. And then in this video we'll cover some of the common things that can happen and we'll talk about how to avoid them.

The links at the top of the video will take you to other troubleshooting tutorials available to subscribers to Knit it Now. Whether you're a new knitter or using a new machine for the first time, one of the first things you must know is how to remove the carriage from your machine in the middle of a row.

If for some reason the carriage jams while knitting, don't force it. Serious damage can be caused by a knot in the yarn or mis-shaped stitch. Follow your machine manual for the procedure for removing your carriage or opening your carriage to release a jam.

You're knitting along just fine, or maybe you just change colors for a Stripe and all the stitches drop off. More than likely there's no yarn in the feeder for some reason. Maybe the yarn broke or you reached the end of the yarn, replace the knitting in the hooks of the needles or ravel it out and try again.

Now to prevent this from happening, take extra care to confirm that the yarn is in the feeder correctly and watch for knots and the end of the ball or cone of yarn. Now, here's a tip. If you're reaching the end of the cone or ball, be sure that there's at least three times the width of your knitting left, or you'll run the risk of dropping some or all of the stitches off the machine unexpectedly.

If you find that stitches are dropped at the beginning of a row, check the yarn, take-up spring, make sure the yarn is threaded correctly and the Springs not caught up somewhere. With some yarns you will need to take up the Slack in the yarn at the beginning of every row.

Also, be sure you're not taking the carriage too far from the edge of the knitting and causing this extra Slack. Carefully remove the pin each time. You'll have a neat and tidy seam with no guesswork about which strands to pick up try both of these methods and see which one you like. They will improve your sew-as-you-go seaming.

With non-patterning knitting machines, and any time you want to work a hand-manipulated stitch pattern, there's usually a lot of counting of needles involved. For simple stitch transfers, you can use a pencil or a water-soluble pen and simply mark the needle bed.

You could also use your needle pushers to select sets of needles. I found that cheat sheets come in handy for more complicated stitch patterns. We've created a set of sheets for the various gauges of machines. The grids are sized according to the needle pitch.

That's the space between the centers of the needles. Here I'm using a 6. 5 millimeter gauge, and the needles of my LK150 fit exactly in the boxes of the grid. I've marked my stitch pattern sequence in pink. I'll have two needles that will be small cables over three rows, and there will be six needles in between that are going to remain in plain knitting.

As I'm knitting, I just simply line up the appropriate row on the cheat sheet with my needle bed. Pull out the needles according to the chart. I move the cheat sheet along the bed for the width of my knitting, and without having to count needles, I'm now ready to do the hand manipulation.
Download a set of cheat sheets from the Knit It Now website. It includes all the common gauges of domestic knitting machines, from fine gauge to Bulky

Here's a hem or a trim that's unique and cute as can be. It's a little fussy, but not too bad and there are some options for making it your own. It's a double bed edge. I found that a smooth yarn and that shows stitch definition works best.

Set your machine for full needle rib. Your pitch will be H. The tension on both beds set it to about three. Set your machine for full needle rib. Now, even if you normally knit a zigzag, row at zero, don't do that for this one.

We're going to be manipulating the strands and we need them to be a little bit loose, not sloppy, but loose. You'll want to have a multiple of three plus two needles and work on the main bed. The corresponding needles in work on the ribber, along with the two edge needles on the ribber.

Knit the zigzag row, and carefully hang the cast on comb and some weight. Don't knit a circular row. We'll transfer stitches as shown. You'll end up with three stitches on one needle. And two empty needles, three stitches on one needle, and two empty needles.

I started by transferring the stitch on the second needle on the left of the needle bed to its neighbor on the right, and then transferred the next needle back to that same needle, putting three stitches on each needle. This leaves an edge stitch needle for seaming.

Now work these transfers all the way across the bed and make sure all of the needles are in working position. Knit 4 rows. Everything should be knitting. There are no needles and out of work position. Next, repeat the transfers over the same needles in the same order.

Make sure all of the needles are in work again and continue knitting in full needle rib. Can you see the pretty little eyelets that are formed right along the top edge? Now this would be a great edge for a really easy full needle rib scarf.

I don't know about you, but I don't often knit garments and full needle rib, but we can still use this pretty scallop. After you work the two sets of transfers, transfer the ribber needles up to the main bed, but you can continue just knitting single bed from here.

Okay. Another thing to notice is that the trim is quite a bit wider than the stockinette, so you need to plan ahead a bit, cast on your edge with fewer stitches than you need for your garment, and then increase evenly before switching to stockinette.

Now, having said that, I immediately thought about the fact that tuck is wider than stockinette. The tuck I chose is a right side facing design. In other words, the purlside is the right side of the fabric to create the scallop edge.

This time I reversed the technique and I transferred the ribber stitches to form the scallops. And then transferred all the ribber stitches up to the main bed. This way, the public side of the scallop trim was facing me. And as I work the tuck, the public side of the tuck was also facing me.

The tuck stitch gave me more width and took care of the flare that I found when I worked stockinette. I hope you'll give this edge a try. There aren't too many steps and transferring the stitches is well worth it.

A fellow knitter recently showed me a ready-to-wear sweater that she wanted to duplicate. Now, anytime I look at sweaters with my machine knitter's eye, I put them to the test. Can it be done? Our machines have some limitations and we need to keep these in mind.

Is it practical? Some designs just don't lend themselves to our knitting machines. Sweaters knit in the round, for example. Are you willing to do what it takes? One knitter may find it great fun to hand manipulate every square inch of a sweater.

Others, like me, prefer an easier route. Let's take a look at the construction of this sweater and consider these three criteria. This design is a fitted cardigan in a tunic length with short sleeves. It has empire styling and the soft collar frames a very low V neck.

It's difficult to see the armholes in the photo, but I'm guessing it has set in sleeves. It looks like the knitting is plain old stockinette and it has ribbed hems other than the collar. It appears that this sweater meets our first criteria.

Can it be done? Sure. The second criteria is, is this design practical on the machine? Now, it appears that the collar is the only area that could be problematic. Because of our needlebed limitations, we couldn't knit the entire collar and front bands in one piece.

Now that we've established that it's possible, the big question is, are you willing to do what it takes to create this design? First, are you willing to draft the complete pattern from scratch or are you willing to modify an existing pattern?

Here are some options. You could start with a knit it now basic pattern for a cardigan with set in sleeves and use our tools to modify it to create that V neck and the other pieces of this pattern. If you have DesignaKnit, you could create the pattern shapes if you're so inclined.

You could draw the shapes to scale based on the finished dimensions of the sweater and create a design for your knit leader or knit radar. You could also find a hand or machine knitting pattern that is close to this shape and make changes for your design.

Do you have a ribber? If not, the hems could be hand manipulated or knit by hand. Let's tackle the most difficult part of this design, the collar and the neckband. The easiest solution would be to pick up and knit the collar and bands by hand.

Do you hand knit? Are you willing to take time to do it? Now, with a little planning, we could knit the ribbed band and the collar in multiple pieces. It would be important to plan where the seams would be placed and notice that the collar is shaped.

It's wider at the center back, so there would be some short row shaping in the collar area. Hmm. Short rows in ribbing. For me, creating this sweater would be a fun challenge, especially because I love to hand knit. What about you?

When we are machine knitting, the whole purpose of the yarn mass is to keep steady, even tension on your working yarn. But things can go wrong. If you hit a knot or the yarn gets caught up somehow, maybe it gets caught up under the cone.

You might have a few stitches that are misformed and way too tight. The only remedy for this is to rip out to this row and start again. Sometimes after you've ripped or you've done some hand manipulation or changed colors or for whatever reason, the mast isn't engaged in putting the proper tension on your working yarn.

My first knitting teacher taught me to milk the cow. Hold down on the yarn behind the tension mast and make sure that the mast engages, and it will ensure perfectly formed stitches every time. It's a good habit to check. Any time you start knitting, you first sit down to knit or you've gotten up to take a break, make sure that tension mast is engaged and you've got nicely formed stitches.

A fellow knitter, Mary, was lamenting that the Jaggerspun of Maine Mill was closing. She said, I love their Superlamb 4/8. What can I substitute? Now, the best way to find a similar yarn is to first look for the fiber you like.

The Superlamb was 100% superwash wool on cones. Sadly, there are very few choices for us here in the US for any yarn on cones. Let's take a look at yarn on balls or hanks. Yarn is often classified by the Craft Yarn Council numbering system, one through six.

But here are two ways that can be more accurate. First, look at yards per pound. Using the Knitted Now Vintage Yarn Index, we can see that the Superlamb had approximately 1120 yards per pound. Our Yarn Index is a listing of vintage yarns that you can use for reference, especially when using vintage patterns.

Looking at the Knitpicks Wool of the Andes Superwash, it has approximately 110 yards per 50 grams. Using the Knit It Now Yards per Pound Tool, we can calculate that 110 yards in a 50 gram ball is approximately 997 yards per pound.

Comparing a 1120 to 997, we can tell that the Knit Picks yarn will be heavier than what she was using, and it won't give her the same hand or drape she's used to. Let's look at another yarn. Here's an old standby, the Lion brand Wool Ease.

It's listed as having 180 meters in 85 grams. The tool tells us that this is approximately 1,050 yards per pound. Now, this may knit up closer to what Mary had used in the past. The second way to compare yarns is to look at the suggested gauge.

The Wool of the Andes is listed as 18 to 20 stitches to 4 inches, and the Wool Ease is 18 stitches to 4 inches. In addition to the yards per pound, comparing these gauges to what she used with her original yarn will give her even more information to compare.
Using yards per pound and the gauge is much more accurate way of comparing yarn than the Craft Yarn Council numbering system.

Shaping a shallow round neck line for a sweater back can be tricky. I'll knit back to row counter 58. Don't forget to wrap. Knit to the left. Row counter 59 even though my pattern is telling me to bind off three stitches, I really don't want to wrap near that seeming stitch, so I'm going to only hold two stitches this time.

Sometimes it's okay to break the rules, especially when you make a mistake like I just did. Knit across and back. Now because I chose to short row, I've knit one extra row over just a few of those little stitches and that shouldn't be a problem.

We choose to short row to have a smoother seam. One extra row isn't going to hurt. At this point, notice that there are a bunch of wraps on the needles. So I'm going to net one more row to secure these reps and then scrap off.

Now you could scrap off without knitting that extra row, but when you go to rehang this edge to seam the shoulder, you'll have stitches and wraps to pick up at the same time. This is not my idea of fun. Knit an extra row rehang the stitches for the shoulder seam and take out that row.

If it bothers. You again, just one more row isn't going to hurt anything. You might also want to adjust your shaping to match your row counts exactly. If you're that kind of knitter and you must have your row counts exact to the pattern, go for it.

At this point, I'd rather have a nice smooth seam rather than steric steps. Okay. We have one side shaped and scrapped off and the other stitches are still in hold. At this point, you have a choice. But I chose to scrap off those center stitches. No real reason why I did it. Just try it both ways and see what you like. We'll follow our pattern again and work the shaping in reverse. Reset the row counter to 54 check to make sure your carriage is still in hold.

Push all the needles back into working position and then following your first shaping instructions. Put three needles into hold position. Knit across and wrap that end needle. Decrease one stitch and knit to the right. Put three more needles into hold knit across and wrap.

Decrease at the neck edge. Three more needles in hold for the shoulder shaping. KNit left. wrap, decrease, one stitch at the neck edge. You get the idea. Just keep following your pattern and just do the reverse of what you did on the other side.

A fellow knitter, Carmen, wants to knit a cardigan with curved front edges. Now, unlike diagonal shaping, where you can use the magic formula, there really isn't a mathematical formula that can be used to create a deep curve.

Remember, each square represents one stitch and one row. Use a pencil and start drawing a zigzag line across the stitches and rows following the curve. This doesn't have to be perfect. Can you see how this is creating a nice, graceful curve following along stitches and rows?

To make things easier. If you're using a stitch pattern that has colors marked 1-2-3-4. Be sure to arrange the colors in the color changer accordingly. Thread up each color in the color changer. Now, I tried to make this harder than it really is.

All you have to do is push in, say, button 1, and thread the first yarn around the yarn guide and in the groove of the roller. Now, you shouldn't have to struggle. The yarn pops right into place. Continue for each color, I recommend that you peek from the back to make sure there's no hang ups and each of the yarns are correctly in place.

When all four colors are threaded, loop them around and secure them underneath the yarn holder. So now you have your hands free, the yarns are threaded up, and they're secure. My first experiment, I started with no needles in work.

Push your carriage back to the right slowly and confirm that you picked up color 1. Don't go too far right, we don't want to be pulling too much tension off this yarn. I did find that if I tried to knit too quickly, or if I took the carriage too far past the right side of the knitting, I not only distorted the stitches on the right side, but I often got a loop where the yarn got caught up in the mechanism underneath the carriage.

So this takes practice to get the right rhythm and to make sure that everything's working as you're knitting. Like everything else in machine knitting, I discovered there's an art to using this color changer. You need to slow down, confirm the colors, and just take it easy.

It's still a whole lot faster and easier than changing colors manually. Now that you've been successful in knitting stripes, I hope you've been successful in knitting stripes. I encourage you to go back to your manual, the color changer manual, and reread everything.

I found that even though I struggled, all the information I needed was there. I just found it difficult at first. Once I saw how things were supposed to work, it got a whole lot easier. So much fun. And this allows you to do so many things. Now, one thing to note with stitch patterns is that punch card and electronic stitch patterns have to be reversed for working with the color changer. You can see an example in my manual.

Mock ribbing is a great alternative for machine knitters to using a ribber, hand-manipulating, or hand-knitting ribbing. In a previous video, we discussed options for creating beautiful mock ribs. But how do you seam them?

With a little planning, you can have beautiful seams in your mock ribs. Now, one note, you may have to adjust the number of stitches you cast on to work these tips, but you can always adjust your stitch count after you've completed your mock ribs.

Let's take a look at one by one mock ribs. While you're planning your cast on, be sure that you have a stitch on both edges of the knitting. This will be dedicated as a seaming stitch. As you mattress stitch the seam, just pick up half of each edge stitch.

Done neatly, you'll have a whole stitch along that seam, and it will not be noticeable. Remember, you'll want to continue seaming one half of that edge stitch beyond the mock ribbing. For two by one mock ribs, make sure you have two stitches on each end of the knitting.

This time, you'll mattress stitch between the two edge stitches as you normally would with mattress stitch. This will allow you to continue the two stitch pattern repeat across your seam. Three by one mock rib takes a little more planning.

Now, let's say you're using this for a sock or mitten cuff. Set up your mock rib with two stitches on one edge and three stitches on the other edge. When you fold the work to create the cuff, you'll mattress stitch between the edge stitches and still maintain a three-stitch column intact.
If seaming mock ribbing has kept you from using it, please practice these seams. Mock ribbing is a great technique for your machine knitting bag of tricks.

This sock is knit from the heel up to the cuff. We'll start by working an open caston for the heel. We'll be joining these open stitches to the leg later, so cast on with waist yarn and ravel cord. Next, we'll start shaping the heel with short row shaping.

Now, this is automatic wrap short row shaping. Just keep repeating this according to your pattern. Now, if this shaping is new to you, please study the tutorials that are included with this course. Also, please practice this technique before you start knitting your socks.

When the short rows decreases are complete, I'll shortrow increase until all the needles are back into working position. Now that the heel is finished, I'll knit the sole indicated by the letter C on the diagram. This is the bottom of the foot.

When that knitting is complete, we'll knit the toe. Again, we're going to use short row shaping. But this time, notice that I'm using. A manual wrap method. The needles are pulled out into hold on the opposite side of the carriage, and then the yarn is manually wrapped to prevent holes.

These two methods are explored in a tutorial in this course under the heel and toe technique section. Now, if all of this is new to you, please watch, learn and practice both automatic and manual short rows shaping and decide which you prefer.

Now that the toe is done, we'll knit the instep of the sock. This is a great place to get creative with cables or lace or color work. In this example, I put stripes on the instep only. It's a great way to incorporate little bits of yarn.

Now, here's the fun part. Remember those live stitches at the heel? We're going to turn the knitting so that the pearl side of that heel is facing us. And then hang those live stitches on the machine. Just take care that you don't twist the sock.

Take a minute to make sure you can rehang this, either on the left or the right side of the work. It really doesn't matter. We're just joining the heel to the. Leg at this point, eliminating a seam. Now notice that I've doubled up the seaming stitches at the join here.

This will make seaming neater at that join point. Once all the stitches are on the machine, continue to knit the leg in the stitch pattern of your choice knitting pattern instructs you to knit a few rows plain for a transition.

And at that point, feel free to transfer stitches to the river for a ribbed leg or remove the knitting on hand knitting needles. To hand knit some ribbing. I chose to knit a plain leg with a rolled edge. I worked the figure eight bind off for lots of stitch.
Except for the finishing my socks. Done.

Here is an interesting needle-out-of-work tuck stitch that's easy to do and creates a light, open fabric. This technique is often called tuck lace. Sometimes tuck can get a bit heavy and dense. Keeping needles out of work can help to create a more lightweight fabric.

All three of these images are the same swatch. Right side, wrong side, wrong side, the choice is yours. I've cast on over every other needle and knit two rows. Now, remember, tuck needs weight, so not only will I weight my cast on edge, I'll move claw weights up the side of my knitting as it grows.

Following my pattern, I'm manually pulling every-other-needle in work to hold position. Set the carriage to hold and tuck for 4 rows. Then I'll cancel hold and knit one closing row. For the next sequence, I'll keep those same needles in out of work position, but this time I'll pull the opposite working needles into hold.

Make sure my carriage is set to hold, those needles are all the way out into hold position, knit four rows and knit a closing row. Now, alternating the tuck stitches gives the smocking effect that you see. Notice that I'm not tucking the edge needles.

This will give me a good solid edge for seaming. And you can see the little extra weight on those edges really helps. I hope you'll give this stitch pattern a try. It's a pretty one, not hard to do, and will open up your eyes to some possibilities of tuck lace.

A yarn balance or scale is a useful tool to identify the yards per pound of yarn, maybe mistery yarn or a skein of yarn. By knowing the yards per pound, you can more easily compare the weights of yarn, this tool is available from many sources specializing in weaving yarn.

They're available for weighing, yarn in both metric and imperial units. Set up, the scale on a level surface. Set the metal pins into the slots on each side of the box. Now cut a strand of yarn and hang it over the notched edge of the scale with the yarn hanging freely.

Initially, the scale will hang downward from the weight of the yarn. Use a pair of scissors and carefully start trimming both ends of the yarn strand in about half-inch increments until the scale is level. Remove the strand of yarn and then measure it, just stretch it just slightly.

And multiply the inch measurement by 100 to determine the yards per pound. In this example, it measures 9.5 inches times 100 this yarn and would be approximately 950 per pound. Now, here's another tip to determine the amount of yarn remaining on a cone or a ball of yarn, weigh the cone on a kitchen or postal scale, a digital scale, subtract about an ounce for the paper cone.

Divide by 16, the yards per pound, determined by the yard balance, 16 ounces equals one pound. To find the number of yards remaining, multiply the answer by the number of ounces of yarn remaining. Casting on if you are a hand knitter, you probably know that there are lots of different cast-on methods. The same is true for machine knitters. Even in crochet, you often work with a foundation row to get started. There are two basic cast-on types open cast-on's and closed cast-on's.

Open is usually a very quick way of getting started. A provisional type cast on is another somewhat open cast on where you can pick up stitches and finish knitting at a later time. Maybe you'll start your garment on the machine with an open cast on and then pick up the stitches on hand knitting needles and create a pretty ruffle or ribbing by hand.

There are lots of reasons to use an open on. But more often we don't want live stitches, we want a permanent, closed finished edge that will be attractive on its own. Part of the decision on which cast-on method to use is the purpose of your edge.

Will this edge be the finished edge of your garment? Will you be picking up stitches and maybe working a trim? Will you be crocheting around the edge of your item? Will this edge be hidden by something else? There's a lot to consider.

Here's the open cast-on that many beginners are taught. It's good for casting out a few stitches quickly. Make sure your carriage is set to neutral, it's set for plain knitting. Thread the tensioning system in the carriage.

Depending on your yarn, said the carriage tension to somewhere around the middle of the dial. Put 20 to 30 stitches into working position. Holding the tail of the yarn below the carriage with one hand push the carriage across the needles from right to left, your needles should look like this.

If your tension is too loose, the loops are going to be loose and sloppy and they may not form stitches well. Too tight of a tension will cause problems as well. Now, place your ravel cord across the stitches between the needle hooks and the gate pegs.

You don't want the cord in the hooks just next to the hooks. Pull down on the ends of the ravel cord and hold the yarn tail as well. You'll want the cord to be below the needles holding those loops in place now, knit 4 or 5 rows.

Remove the ravel cord. You'll see now why ravel cord needs to be strong and slippery. Continue knitting. Here are the live stitches that are left behind. Now, another negative for this particular method is that it's difficult to use over a large number of stitches.

It's important that you put pressure on the main yarn loops with the ravel cord. So if you have a lot of stitches, it's hard to get that pressure in the middle of the piece. So the stitches knit properly. Let's try a different method.

Many knitting machines come with a cast-on comb. This allows you to quickly work an open cast on over as many stitches as you'd like. As before, Make sure your carriage is set to neutral. The tension is set according to your yarn.

Put 20 or 30 needles into work, thread up your machine and knit across from right to left. Next, hang the teeth of your cast-on comb in the loops of the yarn from front to back. Be sure to catch all the loops so each needle knits properly.

Knit back from left to right. Like the ravel cord, the cast on puts pressure on those loops so the stitches will knit. Did all your stitches knit? Here's a problem, if you look closely, my cast on Combe has some bent teeth, and I didn't catch each loop.

Gauge rulers or gauge scales are not machine-specific, they are stitch and row specific. In a recent Knitclub meeting, UA knitter mentioned that she had gauge rulers, but she didn't know what machine they were for. And this just didn't ring true to me, so we decided to investigate.

Now, I've removed the color from these images so we can examine the rulers themselves. We've marked 20 stitches and 30 stitches on this swatch. Notice that the bottom ruler has the number 30 printed right on it in a circle so we can cheat here and we know that this ruler is gauged for 30 stitches, but the top ruler doesn't tell us how many stitches to measure.

Now, remember, we read the gauge rulers in this direction, so measuring 30 stitches with the bottom ruler, we get 15. Now that translates to 15 stitches to four inches or 10 centimeters. If we read the top ruler at 20 stitches, it also measures 15.

If we use a regular old ruler, 30 stitches measures, eight inches. And if we do the math, we also get 15 stitches to four inches or 10 centimeters. So all three scales, no matter what color they are, no matter what you call them, are measuring the same gauge for my swatch.

The takeaway from this experiment is that no matter what color the rulers are, the top ruler is gauged for 20 stitches and the bottom ruler is gauged for 30 stitches. Now, here's another example, using three different rulers.

Doesn't matter what machine was used to knit the sample. Again, notice that two of the three rulers don't have any kind of indication about what gauge to you they're using or what to measure. The swatch is marked at 40 stitches, 20 stitches and 30 stitches.

Now these are common gauges for these gauge rulers. Using the bottom ruler, 40 stitches, measures out at approximately 27 stitches to four inches or 10 centimeters. The middle ruler measuring against 20 stitches also measures 27 stitches to four inches or 10 centimeters.

And the top ruler at 30 stitches measures the same. And using a regular old ruler, 40 stitches measures approximately eight inches. Doing the math, this confirms that the gauge of the swatch, no matter what ruler we use, is twenty seven stitches to four inches or 10 centimeters.

So does this convince you that these rulers are not machine-specific? They are stitches and rows specific. Also, have you noticed that other than the markers on my rulers, my little cheat sheets, I haven't mentioned the words standard, mid or bulky.

I don't know what machine these swatches were knit with. And it really doesn't matter. What matters is the number of stitches and rows that are measured. If you have a white or purple or a tangerine color ruler, just confirm how it's gauged.

Is it gauged at 20, 30, 40 or maybe even some other stitch count. Once you establish what that is, mark the ruler. So there's no guesswork and you can use this ruler again and again. One last thing. In studying my three gauge rulers, I noticed that the largest number on the stitch side of the rulers is twice the stitch count that the ruler is gauged to.

In other words, the yellow ruler is a 30 stitch gauge and the largest number on that scale is 60. On the 20 stitch gauge ruler, its largest number is 40. On the 40 stitch gauge ruler, the largest number on the stitch scale is 80.
Now, this isn't true on the row side of the scales. Hopefully, this will help you identify any mystery rulers that you have and also convince you that the gauge rulers are not machines specific.

Next, pull a few more stitches to hold opposite the carriage. Knit across and wrap. Do it again on the other side. A few more stitches to hold opposite the carriage knit across, and wrap. A total of four rows have been knitted in the center.

Now repeat this for the total of the 12 rows tha you need for your two inches. On the last row, wrap for the last time and then put the needles opposite the carriage into working position. Cancel. Hold. Reset your row counter and continue following your pattern.

We are planning to knit a cute little drop shoulder tee. Now this could be a child's Pinafore or something else, but the front is knit in one piece and we want the yoke section in a different stitch pattern. Now we know that two stitch patterns are going to have very different gauge.

Let's say stockinette at 20 stitches to four inches or 10 centimeters or seven stitches to the inch. Let's ignore the difference in rows for now. According to the pattern, when we get to the yoke section the knitting will measure 16 inches.

At this gauge, this translates to 112 stitches. We've swatched and we've established that our lace gauge is 24 stitches to four inches, so instead of seven stitches to the inch, we're looking at six stitches to the inch. So if we continue knitting over the 112 stitches and we knit in the lace pattern, the yoke's going to end up being more than 18 inches wide instead of the desired 16 this could make the piece really wonky and not fit.

So what has to happen? When it's time to switch and start knitting the lace pattern, we need to decrease some stitches. How many? 16 inches at six stitches per inch would be 96 stitches, not 112 so we need to decrease 16 stitches evenly.

How would you do that? One way would be to remove the knitting from the bed with a garter bar or scrap yarn and then rehang the work over the 96 needles, doubling up stitches evenly across the bed. Then you could continue knitting in the lace pattern and it would be the right size.

But there definitely will be a road differences as well. Now, if you hate math as much as I do, there's an easier way to calculate how many stitches to decrease and have the row counts and the shaping accurate too. Just build your Knit it Now pattern twice.

Once at each gauge, the pattern will tell you the number of stitches at the stockinette gauge and the number of stitches at the lace gauge. Plus it will give you accurate row counts for the lace section as well, based on your row gauge in lace.

So start knitting with pattern 1at the stockinette gauge and then switch to pattern 2 decreasing stitches according to the pattern and complete the yoke using pattern 2. If you do this, you're guaranteed that your knitting will end up the right size and your sweater will fit.
