Something to consider. For most of the design, both yarns are knitting together at the same time. Be sure to keep this in mind when you're selecting the weights of yarn to combine, this is an interesting fabric, but we can improve on this.

I replaced the thin green yarn with a variegated thread. This is actual quilting thread on cones. I think it's designed for long arm quilting. This is a much more interesting fabric. You can clearly see the individual stitches that are knit with the thread alone.

Here's another example. At this gauge a heavier yarn is jazzed up with the variegated thread. That's the bulky machine. But here's my favorite. Take a look at thread lace on the standard. Same concept, but I really love this.

White sewing thread with a white yarn. White yarn with a colored sewing thread. White yarn with another verigated sewing thread. You can really see how knitting the two yarns together changes the white knitting and it makes it something really special.

Now in the past, this technique has always been demonstrated, being worked with a fine, clear filament. Because the filament didn't have any color. It really does look like lace. But I don't know about you, it never appealed to me.

I couldn't get excited about this technique until I played with sewing thread. Looking at stitch patterns that are good for this technique. You're not going to want too many needles next to each other being selected. Notice that the white square is the heavier yarn.

The black squares represent the finer yarn. So you don't want a bunch of black squares next to each other. Here at the machine, there are four stitches that are knit with the finer yarn, but there's a long float behind. So keep this in mind when selecting patterns to use for thread lace.

I hope you'll give this a try. Thread lace is an interesting alternative to other stitch patterns and plain old stockinette. And I'm sure that you can come up with some other beautiful combinations for your knitting.

You don't have to work increases and decreases at the edge of your knitting. In this example, we're going to increase in the center of the knitting for a bust dart in a sideways knit sweater. We'll be using a garter bar to move a large number of stitches.

Start by marking the needle that will be used for reference. To keep from dropping stitches, hang a three-prong tool on the needles to the left of the marked needle. Just let it hang, remove the group of stitches on the garter bar.

Move them one needle to the right, leaving an emptied needle. Then rehang the stitches from the garter bar. Pick up the butt of a stitch in the row below to fill the empty needle. One stitch has been increased. Following your knitting instructions.

Repeat the increase for as many times as needed for your pattern. To work decreases in the middle of the knitting, start by transferring the Mark stitch to the left, leaving an emptied needle, hanging that three-prong tool will keep the stitches from popping off.

Then remove the group of stitches on the garter bar, shift them to the left, filling in that emptied needle. Take the newly emptied needle to out of work position. And you will have decreased a stitch in the middle of the knitting.
Following your knitting instructions, repeat the decrease for as many times as needed.

Although our knitting machines can't cross cables automatically, using a ribber to create knit and purl stitches of traditional cable knitting makes the process a whole lot easier. For these mini cables, cast on and set the needle arrangement to look like this.

Now I prefer to cross my cables on the main bed, but you could reverse this needle arrangement and cross the cables on the ribber . I also chose to knit six rows between cables, but that's up to you. For a hand manipulated pattern, this one goes pretty quickly and the results are so worth the extra effort.

We often think of pin tucks as horizontal lines across our knitting. But we could do so much more with this technique. To review: pin tucks on the ribber are formed with full needle rib. All needles in work on both beds. One of the beds is set to slip for a few rows while the other bed continues to knit.

The additional rows that are knit will bubble up and form texture. If we slip on the main bed and use punch cards or electronic stitch patterns, we can create lots of different textures. In other words, we don't have to slip an entire row.

Selectively slipping groups of needles on the main bed while continuing to knit the rows on the ribber, we'll create texture like this. Take a close look at this stitch pattern. It's mostly black. The white holes are needles that will be slipping.

Remember, slip stitch means the needle will not knit. And the working yarn will pass UNDER the needle. When knitting on a single bed, this forms floats across the purl side of the fabric, and we often use the stranded side as the public side of our knitting.

Because we're working full needle rib, the ribber's stitches will cover the floats. Texture will form when groups of needles are slipped on the main bed and the ribber continues to knit all rows. In this stitch pattern, I slipped for four rows.

It created diagonal raised areas of texture on the ribber side of the knitting. Looking closely, you can see the distorted slip stitches on the reverse side of the fabric. This is the main bed side of the knitting. Are you starting to see some possibilities?

Here's a more complicated stitch pattern. The needles were selected according to the pattern and slipped. As they were slipped, the ribber needles continued to knit, creating this interesting graphic texture. Depending on your machine and your yarn here are some tips.

It's recommended that you use the fine knit bar on the main bed. This raises the needles slightly and can help with the knitting. Play with the stitch tensions between the beds. If the main bed tension is too loose, those strands can get sloppy and catch on the sinker posts.

I had difficulty with this yarn on my brother, 970. Looking closely, there are sections that are slipping 8 to 10 rows, and I determined this was just too many for my machine with this yarn. In this example, the maximum rows that are slipped are 4.
This doesn't give as much texture, but it knit a lot more cleanly. When choosing or creating a pin tuck pattern, please keep the number of slipped rows in mind for your machine and your yarn.

Take a simple needle arrangement and racking for a beautiful open work lace-like fabric. The needles out of work create the open spaces With this needle arrangement set your ribber to H5 and knit two rows swing to H3 knit to rows and repeat.

Now here's a tip, since we're racking every other row, if you need to stop knitting end with the carriage on the left. That way you won't forget if you've racked or not. When you come back, you'll knit to the right and it'll be time to rack.

I removed my ribber for this sample. And because I was in a hurry, this is just a swatch, I cast on with full needle rib, then dropped the stitches and put needles in and out of work for the pattern. Then continued knitting.

The oops, on the right. If I had used a 7 or a wire weight hanger, this could have prevented the mess. I hope you'll try this technique. Different needle arrangements, different racking sequences will create completely different lace like fabrics.

Going to the extremes of racking, this flat ribs stitch is amazing. With your ribber set to pitch H arrange the needles like this. Notice all needles are and work on the main bed and individual needles are in work on the ribber.

And these will create the zigzag. I've chosen to use every fourth needle, but you can play with different combinations. Think of it this way. We're putting decorative traveling knit stitches on the face of the purl side of the knitting.

Cast on with full needle rib, then transfer the stitches to your needle arrangement. You'll cast on with the ribber set to H0. When your cast on is complete, knit one row from right to left, rack to H1. Knit from left to right.

Rack to H2. Knit from right to left. To H3 knit from left to right. You'll be racking to an even number and then you'll knit left. You'll rack to an odd number and you'll knit right. To complete the zigzag, continue racking all the way to 10 and then work your way back to zero and repeat for the length of your knitting.
The secret of this stitch pattern is the needle arrangement and the extreme racking.

Dealing with floats across the back of our knitting can be a challenge, but we do have lots of options. Yarns strands that are carried across the purl side of the knitting are called floats. We can take advantage of floats with the slip stitch technique.

The strands are carried across the knitting and form decorative patterns against the purl side of the knitting. These examples are just one color slip seen from the purl side. We'll come back to slip in a minute. When working with multiple strands of yarn, especially when working with colors per row, the floats can get problematic.

In garments, we don't want long floats that are easily snagged. So let's talk about some ways of dealing with them. First, if you're knitting a jacket or a coat, a knitted or fabric lining might be the answer. For example, by adding fabric to a blanket, you could use any multicolor stitch pattern without worrying about floats.

For a scarf knit it twice as wide and fold it in half, then neatly seam up the long edge. And again, you can use beautiful Fair Isle designs and hide the floats. Some knitters will latch up long floats as they knit. Just hang the strands, every few rows.

Please consider that this may distort the stitches on either side of the float. But try it for yourself. This is a long-time favorite method for many knitters Another technique that some knitters will use after they're done knitting, is to hand stitch those long floats in place.

Just take another piece of yarn and loosely stitch them down. You'll want to keep your stitching loose and not distort the design. In this example, I'm hanging the long float on a needle before I knit the next row. I'm taking care to keep the needle in working position just looping the strand over.

When I knit the next row, that strand just gets woven in and it doesn't knit. Another idea is to modify the stitch pattern a bit. Reduce the floats for this snowman by adding some snow in the background, just a few random stitches can break up long floats.

This stitch pattern might be better worked as Intarsia. Isolating just the little foot without carrying the stitches to the edge of the knitting. Makes more sense. Instead of dealing with those long floats on the ends. Here I am canceling the end needle selection.

So the contrasting yarn isn't carried to the edge stitches. Since the working yarn is traveling along the edge of the motif, instead of the edge of the knitting, you'll need to be sure to use a separate strand of yarn and wrap the stitches between the motif and the background to prevent holes.

Back to slip stitch. To add some color to your knitting without floats, consider multicolor slip or tuck. Multicolor slip is basically stripes where selected needles are slipped and the color is carried to another row. In this example, the peach color from this row doesn't knit for the four rows of the turquoise, the peach stitches are carried over those turquoise rows, creating a two color stitch pattern with no floats.

The knit side is often used for this technique. Now you won't be knitting, cute little snowman or snowflakes, but this is a method of adding color without dealing with floats at all. Back to the lining idea. Here's a blanket technique for you to consider.

I knit a blanket like this years ago. I don't remember who was the designer. I don't have the original stitch pattern, but this idea can also be applied to other stitch patterns. First, I knit the crayon panel in Fair Isle.

As you can imagine, there were lots of floats. Let's say each crayon section is 40 rows. When the panel was complete, I didn't bind off, but I continued knitting the black color to create a lining. I knit 40 rows. I picked up the edge of that first crayon, knit the row.

Joining the two pieces together. I knit another 40 rows of lining. Picked up the stitches from the edge of the next crayon. Knit the row. Again, joining the two pieces together. I continued doing this until I got to the cast on edge and the lining was complete.

In other words, I made a sandwich. Joining at regular intervals, making a double warm blanket. And hiding the floats. You could do this with any stitch pattern. Think of this as quilting, where you're joining the two layers of knitting as you knit.
We have options when knitting and color incorporate some of these techniques and don't avoid color because of floats.

A full-fashion decrease is a technique where we manipulate stitches, so the decreases form a decorative element. In this video, we'll explore single,fine-tuning double and triple decreases. Please watch to the end where we'll give a tip for fine-tuning this technique.

to work a single full-fashioned decrease, we transfer one stitch, emptying a needle, putting two stitches on one needle, and then we transfer the edge stitches in to fill the empty needle, reducing the number of stitches in work by one, a single decrease.

The extra steps create this decorative element. The decreases can be worked, any number of stitches from the edge. Here, we've decreased one stitch, three stitches in from the edge. Multiple stitches can be decreased the same way with the same decorative full-fashioned effect.

For a double decrease transfer and double up 2 stitches. There are now two empty needles. Then transfer the edge stitches in to fill those empty needles and two stitches are decreased. A triple decrease is worked the same way.

But transferring 3 stitches is really stretching it, so it's best to work a triple decrease in steps. First, take off three of the stitches on a three-pronged tool and rotate the tool to get those stitches and the tool out of the way.

Next, using whatever method works best for you, transfer those edge stitches in. Filling those empty needles. In this example, I'm leaving a 4 stitch edge. Again, transferring those stitches across 3 needles is way too much.

So I'll just transfer a few at a time preventing any stretching or drop stitches. Once all of the empty needles are filled in, I'll rehang those held stitches doubling up. And I've decreased 3 stitches. If you're lucky enough to have a multi-pronged transfer tool, it can make transferring those stitches go more quickly.

Here are the results, we've decreased multiple stitches and created a nice decorative feature. This technique is especially helpful when knitting a European shoulder sweater. This design moves the shoulders shaping to the back of the sweater, and the shaping becomes an integral part of the design1 As you start manipulating the stitches for double and triple decreases.

You'll notice that we're stretching and distorting those stitches. Right off the machine You can see my wonky stitches. plus the edge of the sample is a bit tight. This is just because of how we moved the stitches around. I found that if I manually massage those stitches a bit and worked any slack over to the edge stitch, it not only cleaned up those stretched wonky stitches, but it loosened up the edge as well.

Another tip is to alternate your decreases. if your pattern is telling you to decrease three stitches four times and two stitches three times, alternate the double and triple decreases for a better result. Please give this technique a try on a swatch and try this little tip for perfection and you'll be ready when you need to do double and triple decreases in your knitting.

What is a shawl collar? If you go to the dictionary, by definition, it's a turned over collar of a garment that combines with lapels forming an unbroken curving line. Now as knitters, we usually don't think in terms of lapels, but we do recognize the turned over collar part.

There are a lot of variations of this style of sweater, but I think we can agree that it's a sweater, a pullover or cardigan with an extended band that folds back, forming a collar. Let's look at them from a machine knitter's point of view.

First, let's look at cardigans. This is a shawl collar cardigan, it's just a wide band running from the hem up the front, around the neck, back and down the other side to the other hem. You could use any V-neck cardigan pattern to knit this.

Probably one with a deeper V would work best. There are some considerations. Since the band folds over, we need to knit a reversible fabric like ribbing or garter stitch, or we could knit a double layer band. We can knit the band/collar combination in two ways.

The first way would be a long, skinny band knit in one piece going all the way around the edge of the garment. But traditionally, shawl collars are knit in this direction, working from the garment edge out. As machine knitters we have our needle bed limitation.

But we could knit the band in pieces and then seam the pieces together. Depending on the length of your sweater, you might be able to strategically position the seams at the center back neck or the shoulder seams. Or we could always just pick up that edge and knit the band by hand.

A common variation of a shawl collar cardigan includes a shaped cardigan band. Now, if you're knitting that skinny band lengthwise, you could shape as you're knitting and increasewidth-wise stitches to form the collar. If you're knitting width-wise, you could use short-row to form that collar.

So a shawl collar cardigan is pretty easy to create without any changes to a basic V-neck pattern. Pull over shawl collars are very popular. Again, it's just a band, straight or shaped, knit in a reversible pattern so that it can fold over to form the collar.

The collar and band combination is set into a V neck opening, usually with a squared bottom edge. There are many, many variations on this design. it's popular for small children because the neck opening is large enough to go over the head, but the collar comes up close to the neck for warmth.

The secret to crafting a shawl collar pullover is to make the garment neck opening wide enough to accommodate the collar and to make the neck depth deep enough so the collar can fold over. Looking through your machine knitter's eyes, start examining shawl collar sweaters and ready-to-wear and hand knitting patterns.
You'll be amazed at how many different versions you'll find based on a simple band that folds over to form a collar.

Well, let's take a look at a shawl collar for a pullover. In these two examples, the collar is really high and tight and they look really uncomfortable. Let's take a look at how we can improve these collars. Here's a typical shawl collar neck opening.

It's basically a V neck with a straight bottom. In this example, the bottom is four inches and the neck opening is a typical eight inch. Which would fit my mannequin. If I lay a four-inch wide collar along this edge, we can see that it comes up really high up against the neckline.

If we fold the collar in half, it's still pretty high. That collar is filling in that eight inch neck opening and making it more like a four inch neck opening. And I don't want a turtleneck. By opening up the neck in this example, four or five inches, the angle changes and the folded over collar will fit much better.

The lesson here is you can't use a standard neck opening for a shawl collar. You need to make it wider so that collar will fit. Here's another shawl collar variation, the yellow collar is knit in 2x2, ribbing in a very long, skinny strip.

It meets in the center front when it's folded over the neck, it isn't taking up as much space in the neckline. That skinny band can also be overlapped slightly in the front, but you need to accommodate that overlap in the neck opening.

Here's a wider collar knit in the other direction, also in 2x2 ribbing, it's been blocked heavily. As in the previous drawings, you can see that this collar fills in that neck opening and comes up really high at the neckline.

,ven folded over. It's pretty high and tight. Making the neck opening wider will give the collar more room and it'll be much more comfortable. As machine knitters, we need to consider our needlebed limitations. This piece is 200 stitches wide and it won't go around the neck opening.

I'd need to knit and seam to pieces or knit this collar by hand. There are many, many variations of the shawl collar. Look at this one closely and you can see that it's knit in pieces. The fronts are ribbed in one direction and the back of the collar is picked up, knit the other way.

And then it's seamed. This is a great solution for our needle bed limitations. Also, notice the front edges of this example are shaped, forming a nice deep collar up at the neckline while maintaining a fairly narrow flat V opening.

Knitting socks in the round will eliminate a seam in the foot of your sock. Before we get started, please be familiar with the settings for knitting in the round on your machine. You'll be slipping stitches on one bed while knitting on the opposite bed.

Also, you must swatch for your sock in the round. The gauge will differ from knitting on the single bed. Start by casting on and knitting your ribbing. Unless you want to hand-manipulate your ribbing, you'll be knitting the rubbing flat and then switching to circular knitting.

When the ribbing is complete, transfer all the stitches to the main bed. Drop the Ribber. Now you can knit one plain row if you'd like. Put half of the stitches in hold and scrap off the other half. Notice that I'm scrapping off opposite the carriage, the working yarn is available for the next steps.

This eliminates a yarn tail. Remove your cast on comb and weigths.. Fold the scrapped edge and carefully rehang the stitches on the main bed, doubling up the stitches. Remove the waste yarn. Add some weight. Raise your ribber and carefully transfer one stitch from each needle down to the Ribber.

Yes, this is tedious. There is no shortcut. And before you start knitting, carefully examine the stitches, make sure that they're all picked up, no stitches have dropped and none are crossing the beds. Set your carriages for circular knitting.
Slipping on one bed, knitting on the other, and continue knitting in the round.

Some knitters will choose to use a heavier- than-recommended yarn on their standard gauge machine. Remember, the criteria for the correct yarn to use on your machine has to do with the yarn being able to fit in the hooks of the needles.

And there has to be enough room between the needles. So the stitches form properly. And often-used trick is to knit with every other needle. You still have to swatch, but your swatch may not be knit according to the rules for a standard gauge machine.

Normally, we would measure 40 stitches and 60 rows with a green ruler. For this example, we're going to measure over our choice of stitches and rows and use a regular ruler to calculate our gauge. Take a look at my swatch.

I've marked and measured over 20 stitches. I've knit 60 rows between the row markers. Just looking at the swatch, you don't know what machine I used and you certainly can't tell that I knit this swatch over every other needle.

The point is, no matter what your needle arrangement, we are counting stitches, not needles. Take a look at the same swatch on the machine, I pulled 73 needles and then I put 38 needles into work and put every other needle into out of work position.

I did an e-wrap Cast-on and started knitting. And as I knit, I was forming 38 total stitches and marked 20 to use for my swatch measurement. When I took the knitting off the machine, it didn't look like much. You can see the channels between the stitches and the stitches look really tiny.

I grabbed a swatch by the Cast-on and Bindoff edges and gave it a tug. This reformed the stitches and they look great. Don't be afraid of stretching too much. But with all that tugging and stretching, you must let that poor swatch rest.

At least overnight, before you block it and measure it. To really get a feel for the importance of letting a swatch rest. Please work this exercise. Knit a swatch and measure it right off the machine. Stretch the knitting lengthwise to pop and reform those stitches and measure it again.

You're going to see a huge difference. Let the swatch rest for a few hours and measure again. Let it rest overnight at least, and measure it again, writing down the measurements each time. Then block your swatch treat it as you're going to treat your final garment and measure.

You're going to see a big difference in the gauge each step of the way. I hope you won't be tempted to start knitting based on the gauge of the knitting taken right off the machine without letting it rest. Please don't get confused when you're knitting every other needle.
You're measuring and counting stitches, not needles. So keep that in mind when you're following the knitting instructions as well.

Seed Stitch and Moss Stitch are very popular in the handknitting world. They are reversible and highly textured. These stitches can be problematic for machine knitters since our machines don't form both knit and purl stitches easily.

Seed Stich alternates knit and purl stitches every row. Moss stitch alternates knit and purl stitches every other row. If you are lucky enough to have a brother standard gauge machine with a G-carriage, the turtle can make quick work of the stitch pattern.

For small sections, hand manipulation is an option. For Seed Stitch, reform every other needle, every other row alternating the stitches. For Moss Sttich reform every other needle, every two rows, alternating every two rows.

If you have a Ribber, you might consider transferring the Seed or Moss Stitches between the beds to form the knit and purl stitches. Either way, when you're hand manipulating this type of stitch pattern, it can be time-consuming, but given in small doses, it can be well worth the effort.

A knitter asked, can I use this card for any stitch pattern? What do you think? Well, let's go back to the function of a punch card. If you have an electronic machine, the ideas here are the same. The black holes tell the machine which needles to select.

What happens to the stitches on those needles depends on your carriage setting. I happen to know that this stitch pattern was designed for a G-carriage, also called an automatic knitting carriage. These were made for the Brother, Knit King, standard gauge machines.

The knitting will look like this. Can you see both knit and purl stitches? But what if we tried to knit this as a tuck stitch? We can't knit tuck needles side by side. Remember how Tuck stitch is formed. The yarn loops over the needles and needles right next to each other will get great big loops and just make a mess.

So in viewing this card, we can immediately see that there are holes side by side, not good for tuck. The same thing goes for slip. Slipping lots of needles side by side will create really long floats. Again, remember how slip stitches formed.

The working yarn is carried under the needles, forming floats. Short floats can be decorative. But this row is 24 stitches wide and we'd have a 24 stitch float. Think of free pass where there's no needles knitting. Could this stitch pattern be used for Fair Isle?

Well, I suppose, but every other row would be yellow in this case and the blue would be carried across. Again, really long floats and it's not particularly attractive anyways. So the bottom line, can you use this card for other stitch patterns?
No. You can tell by examining the position of the holes on the stitch pattern.

Adding cables to a knit, maybe just the designer touch you need. Just like any other stitch pattern, cables impact the gauge of your knitting and gauge can only be determined by swatching. Now, before you leave me. Hang in there.

I do have a shortcut. Before we get to the shortcut. If you are planning an all-over cable sweater, for example, just like any other stitch pattern you have to swatch. Think about it. As you're crossing the cables, you're not only impacting the width of your knitting, but the length as well.

Cables are going to shorten the knitting. The difference in rows is really obvious in this swatch. Can you see how much shorter that center cable section is in this small swatch? Imagine the difference over an entire sweater.

In my humble opinion, this little swatch isn't enough to establish gauge for an overall cable sweater. I really need to knit a larger swatch. Now, I won't go on and on and on about swatching. I think I've gotten my point across.

On to the shortcut. The rule of thumb for cables is that they take 10% to 15% more stitches than plain knitting. So let's say we want to run a single cable up along the edge of our cardigan or maybe a single cable down the center of a scarf.

I know you're probably not going to want to swatch in this case. So if you've swatched and established stockinette gauge, just add a few stitches for the cable. Again, 10% to 15% more stitches. Comparing my two swatches, both have 20 stitches between the markers.

I'll need to add 6 stitches or so to my garment to account for these cables. So if my pattern tells me to cast on 100 stitches, I would cast on 106 stitches. So the front piece is going to end up being the right size. I'll have to block the cable section heavily for length, or I might consider a few short rows to add length to that cable section.
So when adding cables to your knits, keep in mind that they really impact your gauge, both stitch and row gauge and plan accordingly.

This puffy stitch technique was shared by Julie in our subscriber forum, it produces a thick, squishy fabric on the standard gauge machine without any hand manipulation. It's really best worked on an automatic patterning machine, although you could select needles for every row.

The stitch pattern is simply a 1x1 pattern. You could use this design or lock a design with every other stitch being selected. The object is to slip the same needles throughout the pattern repeats. The texture comes from slip stitch, remember, with slip stitch, the working yarn passes under the needles being slipped.

You'll slip every- other-needle for 9 rows. And then knit one row plain across all of the needles. Slip every other needle for 9rows and then at one row over all of the needles. Repeating this gives you raised puffy ridges on the purl side and creates a thick fabric.

Now you can play with the number of rows, but be sure to be consistent and keep the repeats to an even number. Looking at the knit side, you can see how every other stitch has been slipped. This stitch pattern has a lot of stretch width-wise, but it's really quite stable lengthwise.

Julie used the stitch pattern for a nice thick cover on a clothes hanger. She also suggested using it for slippers. Again, it's a great way to get a thick, comfy fabric from a standard gauge machine. For Brother knitters set up your stitch pattern, either electronics or punch card.

Set the KC knob so the machine reads the stitch pattern. Push in both part buttons and knit 9 rows. The part buttons will be doing the slipping. Disengage the part buttons and knit one row plain. Do it again, push in both part buttons, knit 9 rows.

Disengage the part buttons again and knit one row. And keep repeating for as long as you need the piece. Because you're building up those raised ridges, it's going to take a lot of rows to create any length. For Silver Singer, Studio knitters, set-aside levers to knit in pattern.

Engage your electronics or lock your punch card to select every other needle. Set the cam lever to slip and knit 9 rows. Set the cam lever for plain knitting, knit one row. Cam lever to slip knit 9 rows.Cam lever for plain knitting in one row.
Repeat for the desired length. Have fun with this puffy stitch technique and be sure to share how you've used it.

My knitting instructions are telling me to increase stitches evenly across the row. In this sample, I've removed the knitting from the machine and then I'm rehanging the stitches, leaving empty needles. The first method is a hand knitting technique called knit in the front and back.

Transfer tools have a number of uses. Here are the basic steps for transferring stitches. With the single prong tool, place it over the hook of the needle. Pull the tool and the needle back, allowing the stitch to fall behind the latch.

Push the tool and the needle forward. The stitch should automatically close the latch. Keep pushing until the stitch slips off the needle and transfers to the tool. To replace the stitch on a needle to create an eyelet or work a decrease, place the hole of the tool over the hook of the new needle.

Tilt the tool up and allow the stitch to slip onto that needle. When the stitch is securely in the hook of the needle, remove the prong of the tool. Use the same steps to use a two, three, or multiprong tool. Place the tool over the hooks of the needles to be transferred, pull out the tool and the needles until the stitches are behind the latches.

Push back to close the latch and slip the stitches onto the tool. Tilt the tool up and replace the stitches as needed. Be sure to put the emptied needles into working position and you can continue knitting. In this example, I left the empty needle in out of work position.
When I knit across, the yarn traveled between the stitches. I then put the needle in work and continued knitting. But you can see that I have an extra-large eyelet.

A latch tool, also called a Tappet tool, is just a machine needle with a handle. It has a number of different uses to manually form stitches. Most commonly, it's used to reverse stitches, turning knit stitches into Purl stitches.

Notice how the Purl bump is showing against the knit stitches in this example. To reform an existing stitch, push the tool into a stitch below the one that's currently in work on a needle. Drop the stitch off the needle and un-ravel it.

Forming a ladder. Use the tool to pick up each ladder, forming new stitches. To create a column of reformed stitches, drop a single stitch. Pick up each ladder, forming new stitches. When the last strand has been knit, rehang the stitch on the needle.

Now you have a column of reformed stitches. This can be done across a row for a turning row or a manually formed decorative Purl row. Another use of the latch tool is for binding off. Knit the last row of your knitting at the loosest tension or manually knit a loose row.

Slip the first stitch off the needle and place it on the tool behind the latch of the tool. Slip the adjacent stitch to the tool in the hook on the tool. Purl the second stitch through the first. This is called a stitch through stitch Bindoff.

This method is fast, but it may not be as stretchy as you need. Please try other bind off methods in addition to this one. Any time you use a latch tool, remember you're positioning a needle in the opposite direction of the needle on the needle bed.
If you reform stitches, they will be facing the opposite way. Think about knit and Purl stitches, as in hand knitting.

When using automatic stitch patterning, we don't want to distort the edges of our knitting. By taking time to ensure that the edge needles knit and not pattern will make it easier to seam piece and to work increases and decreases.

For example, when knitting tuck or slip, we don't want those edge stitches to tuck or slip. When knitting with a lace carriage, we certainly don't want the edge stitch to be an eyelet. Preventing the edge stitches from patterning is important and it's done differently depending on your machine.

On this Singer machine, with this stitch pattern, I can't easily predict when a tuck is going to occur on the edge stitch. Here I can see the tuck stitches on this row and the edge stitch is knitting correctly. But on this row the pattern is trying to tuck the end needle.

By tucking the edge stitch, the knitting will be distorted. To prevent this, put the end needle, maybe two needles into"D" position or pull them all the way out every row. This will prevent those stitches from tucking or patterning.

Now when I work a decrease, I'll have two plain stitches and I'm not messing around with tuck strands on the edges. If you look closely, the tucked edge will be more difficult to seam where the plain edge will be neater and easier to seam.

When knitting in pattern we don't want to distort the edges of our knitting. By taking time to ensure that the edge needles knit and not pattern, it will make it easier to seam the pieces and to work in increases and decreases.

For example, when knitting tuck or Slip. We don't want the edge stitches to tuck or slip. When knitting with a lace carriage, we certainly don't want the edge stitch to be an eyelet. Preventing the edge stitches from patterning is important.

Different machines handle this differently. Some Brother machines allow you to cancel. end needle selection with a setting on the underside of the carriage. This is the Brother 260. For other Brother machines, the change knob also called the KC knob, controls the selection of the end needles.

With the change knob set to KC1 one, the end needles will automatically stay in D or middle position. For example, in this slip stitch pattern, the needles that are in B position will slip. Here, I've set the change knob to KC 2 and the end needle is being selected and will slip.

And you. Can see how this will distort the edge. Looking at tuck, the same thing applies. We don't want to tuck the edge stitch or stitches. With the edge being plain, it will not only be easier to seam that edge, but when shaping increases or decreases, you won't be dealing with a tuck or slip strand.

Because Brother machines preselect the needles. We also have the opportunity to position any edge needles so they don't pattern. Just position them into "D" position before you. Knit the row to manually keep the edges clean.
End needle selection is important when working in pattern to obtain neat edges for seaming and for making shaping easier and neater as well.

As with most things in machine knitting there are many ways to add a folded band to a sweater. Let's take a look at one method of adding a plain stockinette band to some fairisle knitting. This sample represents the front of a cardigan.

In a real project. For accuracy, I would measure the front edge and then I'd establish my stitch gauge in stockinette. Multiply the length of the front by my stitch stitch gauge. And I'll know exactly how many stitches to pick up.

For this sample, I'm simply holding the knitting up to the needle bed, and. I'll pick up approximately three stitches for every four rows. With practice, you'll be able to eyeball. This. With the WRONG SIDE facing. I'll hang both edges and then the center.

I'll continue to divide the sections in half, hanging the stitches neatly. Be careful when picking up. I didn't look closely before I started knitting, and you can see the hole. This was caused by hanging the same. Space in the knitting on two needles side by side.

So don't do as I did. Double check the stitches before you start knitting. Grading the band is helpful in keeping it from flipping out. Knit the inside or the private side of the band at a slightly tighter. Tension than the outside or the public side.

This will force the band to curl towards the inside slightly. Knit the first section of the band, and then knit a turning row. I just knit one row at a very loose tension to create a crease. Then knit the second side of the band.

Let's look at two ways to secure the band. First, pick up the edge stitches and hang them on the needles. And loosely bind off these stitches. Now, I don't prefer this method. It adds bulk and it's difficult to get the bind off just right.

Not too loose and not too tight. The second method is to scrap off the band stitches. Since I'm going to be hand stitching. Those live stitches, I knit a row Of ravel cord and then scrapped off in yarn. I find it easier to stitch from.

The cord instead of from the yarn. With the live stitches secure, it's time to close up this section of the band. I'll just whip stitch those live stitches in place. I suggest you practice both methods and see what you prefer.

Adding ribbed bands with the machine can be a challenge. If you prefer ribbed bands, take it step-by-step and you'll be happy with the results. The key to this is that knitting with the ribber, we must have even weight on the stitches.

We do this with a ribber cast on comb. This is the trickiest part of this method. Start by establishing how many needles you'll need for your band. Keep in mind that ribbing pulls in, so plan ahead accordingly. On the main bed, cast on with waste yarn, cast on over every other needle and hang the ribber cast on comb in the loops.

Knit a few rows of waste yarn and then knit a row of ravel cord. With the wrong side facing. Hang the edge of your cardigan on the needles. After hanging the stitches, it's good practice to close the latches. Using the main bed carriage, knit one row.

The ribber is not in work yet. Next, raise your ribber and attach the ribber connecting arm. Transfer stitches down to the ribber in the needle arrangement of your choice. I chose to knit 2x2 ribbing. Thread up the ribber carriage and knit the number of rows needed for your band.

Then transfer the ribber stitches up to the main bed and loosely bind off. Use the bind off method of your choice. When the band is complete, remove the cast on comb and the waste yarn. And you have a beautiful ribbed band on the machine.

When you're knitting on a standard gauge machine like this, you might find that a single layer of ribbing is too thin. So knit twice the number of rows. Fold the band in half for a doubled band and secure that bind off edge with a whip stitch to the front edge of the sweater.
A single band may work for a bulk or midgauge yarn. You need to test to see what you like best.

Let's create a button band with a beautiful edge finish. This method can use any needle arrangement. I chose to knit my band in full needle rib. Knit the band separately with a nice tubular cast on and then attach it to the front garment edge.

Start by establishing the number of needles needed for your edge. Cast on using the method of your choice. I'm using my favorite Broken Toe Cast On. Once the cast on is complete, set up for the needle arrangement of your choice and knit the number of rows for your band.

Transfer all the stitches up to the main bed and knit one row. Knit a row of ravel cord and scrap off. Now set that band aside and with the right side facing, rehang the garment edge, pushing it back behind the latches. Next, pick up the band stitches with the wrong side of the band facing you.

Place these stitches in the hooks of the needles. When all the stitches are on the machine, close the latches and pull the band stitches through the garment edge and loosely bind off. This bind off is a bit bulky. You may want to use a sewn or a backstitch bind off instead.
By knitting the band separately, we can take advantage of that beautiful cast on edge for the edge of our band.

Let's review how we transfer stitches manually. Using the double-eye needle, we position it opposite the ribber and insert the hook of the needle in the hole of the tool. Pull up the needle and put the stitch behind the latch.

Push down on the needle to slip the stitch onto the tool. Then slip the stitch to the other end of the tool. Position the eye of the tool over the hook of the target needle and slip the stitch off. Now we can do the same thing by using two transfer tools.

Position the eyes of the first tool over the needles to be transferred. Pull up to get the stitches behind the latches. Push down to transfer the stitches to the tool. Insert the prongs of a second tool in the stitches and transfer the stitches to the second tool.
Set the first tool aside. Slip the eyes of the tool over the hooks to the target needles and slip the stitches onto the needles.

The Shadow Lace Transfer Tool, also known as Jaws, is a handy device for transferring stitches between the ribber and the main bed. It was originally designed for Silver / Singer / Studio machines for a technique called shadow lace.

Most knitters use Jaws when transferring a large number of stitches between the beds, instead of just using a double eyed needle and transferring stitches one at a time. Before working with the tool, let's review how we transfer stitches manually.

Using the double eyed needle, we position it opposite the ribber and insert the hook of the needle in the hole of the tool. Pull up the needle and put the stitch behind the latch. Push down on the needle to slip the stitch onto the tool.

Then slip the stitch to the other end of the tool. Position the eye of the tool over the hook of the target needle and slip the stitch off. And we can do the same thing by using two transfer tools. Position the eyes of the first tool over the needles to be transferred.

Pull up to get the stitches behind the latches. Push down to transfer the stitches to the tool. Insert the prongs of a second tool in the stitches and transfer the stitches to the second tool. Set the first tool aside. Slip the eyes of the tool over the hooks of the target needles and slip the stitches onto the needles.

Keeping these visuals in mind, try transferring with Jaws. Each side of the tool is numbered. There's a number one and a number two. Some jaws have two colors. Start by making sure that the latches of the needles on both beds are open.

Position the holes of side one over the needles to be transferred. Think of this as positioning that double-eyed needle. The way Jaws is constructed. We can peek down between the sections of the tool, watch and confirm that the eyes are lining up with the needles and that stitches are transferring.

Pull up to move the stitches behind the latches, push down and rotate the tool so you can transfer the stitches to the tool. Here you can see the stitches are no longer on the ribber needles. But I missed one, so I'll just pick that stitch up and transfer it to the tool.

Here's where that name Jaws comes in. Close the tool and transfer the stitches to side 2. Shift the tool and position the eyes of side two over the main bed needles. Rotate the tool and pop those stitches onto the new needles.
Keep in mind the process is like using the double-eyed needle, but with Jaws, you're transferring a number of stitches at a time.

Because Brother machines pre-select needles prior to knitting, we can check our stitch pattern and the position of the pattern on the needle bed. Without any yarn pass the carriage to examine the needle position. In this example we'll look at the first few rows, start with enough needles in work to accommodate the stitch pattern repeat.

This is stitch pattern #90 and it's a 24 stitch repeat. So I've put 60 needles into working position. The pattern is set for an all-over design. It will repeat across the needlebed. Keep in mind that by default it will be centered on the needle bed in this case, needles 1 through 12, left and right of the imaginary 0.

With the change knobs set to KC (I) or KC (II) take the carriage all the way out past the turn mark, then pass the carriage across the needles. I've double-checked and it's these needles that we'll be for the heel of the boot and they've been selected.

Needles number 5 through 11 and there are repeats across the bed. Pass the carriage back for row 2 and confirm that these needles are selected. On row 3 Again, read your pattern and you should be able to see that these needles are selected.
Can you see the value in dry knitting? No guesswork. You know where the patterning is going to occur even before threading up the machine.

Plaiting or plating is a technique that uses two strands of yarn held together. The machine positions the yarn in such a way that the strands are knitted together at the same time, but one strand shows on the purl side, the other strand shows on the knit side.

Keep in mind that you're knitting two strands together, so you'll want to use a finer yarn than you might normally use on your machine. Also, mixing weights and textures of yarn can produce very interesting plaiting results.

In this plaiting example, the teal is showing on the purl side and the white is showing on the knit side. Think of the possibilities of having reversible fabric, color wise. Without using a plaiting yarn feeder. The yarns would normally twist and the colors would randomly be shown on each side of the knitting.

To knit in plaiting on Brother standard gauge machines, we need to replace the yarn feeder assembly that's in the sinker plate. Remove the sinker plate from the machine. Loosen and remove the screws holding the assembly. If they're tight, use a screwdriver or a coin to loosen them.

With the screws removed, carefully slip the yarn feeder out and insert the plating feeder and secure it with the screws. To thread the feeder, snap one yarn into the back slot and insert the other strand in the front slot.

The feeder positions the yarns so they align in a way that one strand is held in front and shows on the purl side. The other strand shows on the knit side. Plaiting can also be done with the ribber using a ribber plaiting attachment.
Don't forget, since you're knitting with two strands, you'll need to use finer yarn than you might normally knit with.

Do you have trouble with the edge stitches dropping when using your Brother lace carriage? There's a little known and undocumented adjustment to the lace carriage that controls end-needle selection. Turn your lace carriage over and examine the pink lace cams.

Be sure the slot in the screw is vertical. This will prevent the machine from selecting the edge needles. And the lace carriage will not attempt to transfer that edge-stitch. No more dropped edge-stitches.

If you are familiar with knitting slip stitch patterns on the single bed, multi-colored slip is the next logical step. While knitting in slip selected needles do not knit and the working yarn travels under the needles creating floats on the purl side of the knitting.

By changing colors every two rows, a design is created on the knit side of the knitting, allowing multiple colors across the row. The slip stitches are carried across the alternating colors, creating interesting graphic elements.

The best way to understand multicolored slip is to knit it in two contrasting colors and examine the stitches that are slipping. You don't need a color changer to knit 2-color slip. You could manually change the yarn every two rows to get an idea of how this works.

When knitting traditional double bed jacquard. The stitch pattern is worked on the main bed and controlled by the automatic patterning device, punch card or electronics. At the same time, needles are in work on on the ribber creating a backing and it covers any floats from the stitch pattern.

Because the yarn colors are changed every two rows. Stripes are formed on the back of the knitting. To alter the striped effect. Settings are changed or a special carriage is used that automatically selects every other needle on the ribber.

The key is to have an even number of needles in work. The needles to slip are alternated every other row. On Brother machines, you'll use the lili buttons. The official name of these buttons are the ribber Change knobs. Silver Singer machines use a separate bird's eye carriage.

Look closely and you can see the slipped ribber needles. Something to keep in mind is that this technique not only changes the appearance of the backing, but it also distorts the front of the knitting. Give it a try with your stitch pattern to see the results.
Bird's eye backing will also change the gauge of your knitting. So if you're going to use birds eye, be sure to swatch with that technique.

Using cheat sheets when hand manipulating stitch patterns on a manual machine is a great way to keep track of the stitch transfers without counting needles or making yourself crazy. Watch as we knit this simple lace pattern pattern with the Knit it Now cheat sheets.

Based on this hand-knitting stitch diagram, I reproduced the stitch symbols on my sheet. The circles are eyelets which translate to an empty needle for machine knitting. The slants represent the direction of the stitch transfers.

Remember, as machine knitters, we're looking at the knitting from the purl side. Let's start on row one of the stitch pattern. First, I'll orient the chart to the right of the needles in work. According to the chart, I'll skip the first three needles and then I'll transfer the fourth stitch left and empty the needle, creating an eyelet.

Moving across the row, I'll transfer the next eyelet left. Notice that I've highlighted the eyelet column to keep myself oriented. Also notice that I'm working a simple stitch transfer that will look like this. Another option is to work this transfer in two steps.

First picking up the stitch, transferring it right, then picking up both stitches to fill the emptied needle. The difference is subtle and it is equivalent to a right leaning decrease in hand knitting. Right leaning as seen from the knit side of the work.

I'll continue to transfer across the row by moving and positioning the eyelet symbols. Here, I'm lining up the symbol with the existing eyelet, positioning the next symbol for the next transfer. Shift the chart and line up the symbol with the eyelet across the rows.

To double check you can always count the boxes on the chart and count the needles. Once the transfers are complete. My pattern is telling me to knit two rows. But wait a minute. Oops! I didn't put the empty needles into working position and they didn't form the eyelets properly.

I'll need to rip out this row and free pass back and then put all needles in work and continue knitting. For the next row, I'll hold up the next row of my chart using the orange highlighted column and the three needles orientation.

I'll transfer according to the chart. One stitch on the left of the original eyelet column and one stitch on the right. Again, I'm working a simple stitch transfer on the left, but this time I'm working a two step transfer on the right.

This will form a left-leaning stitch. When looking at the knit side of the knitting. I'll continue to work the second row of transfers across the row using the orange highlighted column to orient the chart as I go. This time you can see that 2- step transfer more clearly.

Remembering to put all needles in work this time, I'll knit four rows, creating the eyelets. The next sequence of transfers are positioned between the previous ones. Line up the chart using the three stitches on the right and the orange highlighted column to position the chart.

Remember, the orange column represents that first eyelet on the first row. Transfer left as indicated on the chart, keeping the yellow highlighted column aligned with the new eyelet. Transfer the next eyelet. Count needles if you like and use the orange column to stay oriented.

Slide the chart left and finish the sequence. Notice I'm not transferring along the edge of my piece. I don't want eyelets right on the edge of my knitting. With all needles in work, I'll knit two rows to complete that set of eyelets.

Finish the sequence by counting needles on the right and aligning the yellow highlighted column with the previous eyelet. Transfer left and right of that center eyelet. Keeping the chart aligned, transfer the next set of stitches and repeat across the row.

Keep using that yellow highlighted column to confirm the position of the chart and transfer the last set of stitches. Take time to confirm the accuracy of the position of the eyelets and transfers, and knit four rows. When looking at the knitting from the purl side, it's difficult to see the right and left-leaning transfers.

I suggest you experiment with the appearance of each and use the appropriate technique to get the results you want. Remember, a two-step transfer will lean in the direction that the doubled-up stitches are transferred in relation to the eyelet.

For a simple stitch pattern like this, you might want to choose to work simple transfers because the appearance of left and right leaning isn't as noticeable. The beauty of this stitch are the eyelets, But be aware of the differences with more complex stitch patterns.

Watch as we step through knitting a basic short row sock knit from the toe-up. To keep things simple, I chose to use a solid color. But I'll bet that you can be a whole lot more creative with your yarn, color and stitch pattern choices.

The first place to start is to knit a swatch and establish your gauge. Without an accurate gauge, how do you know how many stitches to cast on and how many rows to knit? Knit a Swatch. 'Nuff said. One of the reasons to knit a toe-up sock is to control of the amount of yarn you need.

There's nothing worse than running out of yarn part way through the second sock. With a little planning that won't happen to you. Weigh the amount of yarn you have in grams. I'm starting with 168 grams. We'll come back to this number later.

Next, plan out the size you want to knit. Measure the foot length and the foot circumference. Determine how long you want the leg. Depending on the amount of yarn you have, you may need to adjust the leg length. Again this is a reason for knitting toe-up.

Once you know your measurements, enter them and build your Knit it Now. Dynamic Pattern. Before doing anything else, read through the entire pattern. Identify anything you might not understand, and look for techniques that you may need to practice.

In the READ ME section, we discuss the placement of the toe seam and knitting a right and left sock so the seams end up on the inside of the legs. Okay, let's get knitting. Scrap on the Toe stitches. I used a green crochet cast-on rag and knit a row of ravel cord.

This will leave open stitches that I can graft later to complete my toe. We'll knit one row and then short row shape the toe according to the pattern instructions. If you aren't completely confident how to knit a sock toe or heel, there are videos available showing some options.

Please take time to watch the videos. Once the toe is complete, scrap on the remainder of the stitches needed for the foot. The "K" dimension in the pattern. I've used a crochet cast-on rag again and one row of yellow ravel cord.

Leaving open stitches that will be grafted to the previous cast-on edge to complete the toe. With all the foot stitches now on the bed, knit the foot section. You may want to add a stitch pattern or change colors. Remember, get creative.

Notice that I added some markers along this long edge to make it easier to seam later. Once the foot is complete, scrap off the first heel stitches. Short rows the Heel. This is exactly like the toe short row process rehang the scrapped off stitches.

I left my waste yarn in place, but you can remove it to make sure you've picked up all the stitches. Note the stitch count on your pattern to double-check. Knit a few rows according to the pattern. I like these extra few rows between the foot and the cuff for the ribbing.

They seem to make a better fitting sock. Now that the foot is complete, weigh and record how much yarn you have left and we'll tell you how much yarn the foot used. It's time to knit the cuff, leg or ribbing. You have lots of choices if you want the whole cuff in ribbing, you can hand-manipulate some ribbing or hang a ribber cast-on comb and transfer stitches to the ribber.

I chose to remove the knitting on a circular hand knitting needle and hand knit the ribbing. Before starting to knit my ribbing, I grafted the toe stitches. If you aren't fussy, you could just pick up both sets of stitches and bind off.

Because the seam can be a little bit bulky, it's best if you plan to have the toe seam on the top of the toes for comfort. I plan to knit my ribbing in the round, so I used mattress stitch to join the side seams, matching up the yellow markers.

While I was knitting the ribbing, I kept track of how much yarn I had remaining. I started with 168 grams. The foot used 34 grams. Now that I'm close to my desired leg length, I'll weigh the ball again and confirm that I have enough yarn remaining.

Or maybe I can knit the leg a little bit longer. My leg used 14 grams. So far I've used a total of 48 grams and have 120 left. No worries about running out. I'm going to make my leg a little bit longer and add a rolled edge.

Instead of worrying about a stretchy bind off in ribbing, I'm going to knit a few rows in, stockinette and then just let it roll. This is a quick way of adding some style to my sock, and I'll have a stretchy bind off. It might seem like socks are complicated, but with a little planning and taking it step-by-step, they're not hard.
I hope you'll give toe-up socks a try. You'll be glad you did. Happy sock knitting.

Let's walk through knitting a Swan Sock. The construction of this sock is unusual, but it's not hard if you focus on each section one at a time. We'll start at the leg or ribbing and then knit the heel, sole and toe, ending with the instep.

Because the sole and instep are knit separately, the sock allows for a lot of creativity with color and stitch patterning. For my sample, I've changed colors for each section to help make things more clear. Instead of ribbing, I just cast on with waste yarn and ravel cord and knit a one inch hem in the dark blue color.

After knitting the ankle in light blue, I scrapped off half of the stitches. We'll pick these up again later and join them to the instep stitches to finish the sock. Next in dark blue is the heel flap, the original pattern.

Suggest using a heel stitch or eye of partridge stitch for a bit of padding and durability. With your first sock I highly suggest knitting that heel flap plain for now. Next, in light pink is the heel turn. If you've knit a sock heel before, this is just one half of a normal heel or toe.

Now the fun starts with knitting the gusset. In light blue I cast on the wings of section five. To make this easier, I've used two small yellow cast on rags and a row of ravel cord. With this in place, I can double eWrap and knit the cast on cleanly with weights on the new stitches.

The light blue gusset section is shaped with decreases to create those wings. Next is the sole of the sock. You can get creative in the center part of the gusset and the sole section, like this red and white version, adding a bit of Fairisle with small floats.

But again, I suggest knitting a plain sock first to get a feel for the overall construction before adding any stitch patterns. My toe is dark blue. Nothing fancy, just short row decreases and increases to form the toe pocket.

To finish the knitting, I switched to dark pink and knit the instep. After scrapping off with orange and using a little steam. How is this going to become a sock? First, the instep is joined to the ankle with kitchener grafting joining the orange scrapped off edges.

The cast on wings are sewn to the heel flap and the instep, sole and gusset are joined along the red dotted lines. This may not be the prettiest sock ever, but it's a good exercise for following each one of the steps in this unusually constructed sock.

And I wanted this to be 78 CM across and I want the length to be 50. Let's move this sleeve out of the way with our right mouse button. And let's move this dress over here. And we'll move this sleeve out of the way. As we'll so you can see, we still can arrange more garments.

We have up to 16 garment pieces available to our garment shape, which is quite a lot of piece. If I knit this up to the top and then I take this off on waist yarn and then put it back, two stitches on every needle, then I can start knitting up the bodice and knit the bodice direction straight up to the top.

A peasant heel in hand knitting refers to a sock heel that is shaped with decreases. Instead of short rows. It is knit in the round. For machine knitters, shaping on the ribber is do-able but tedious, and here's a single bed faux peasant heel that's a combination of decreases and sew-as-you-go.

For this sample, I used a cast on rag and a row of ravel cord. Casting on the number of heel stitches in my pattern, I knit one row before knitting back, I hung a bobby pin over the working yarn. Then, working my decreases on both sides, I used a two-step decrease three stitches from the edge.

After the decreases are done, I held the pin so the yarn stays tight, and the pin isn't picked up by the knitting carriage and knit to the right. Before knitting back, I hung another bobby pin on the working yarn. Holding the pin to keep the thread tight and the pin away from the carriage, I knit back.

This sequence is repeated, decreasing every other row for the number of decreases indicated in the pattern. On the carriage side, hang a pin, work the decreases, knit across, hang a pin and knit back. When the decreases are complete, I'll start the sew-as-you-go to form the heel and toe pocket.

Opposite the carriage, hang the loop being held by the pin on an empty needle, knit across. Opposite the carriage, hang the loop on the next empty needle and knit across. Keep repeating this until the original number of needles are back in work.
The decreased side looks like the hand knit version, and the sew-as-you-go technique makes the shaping go fast with no Kitchener stitch.

Faux ribbing is a tuck stitch pattern that resembles ribbing on the knit side. It's not stretchy like ribbing, it just mimics the texture of 2x1 ribbing. I'm showing the stitch pattern on a manual machine using the hold setting.

But it can also be worked on an automatic patterning machine with this stitch pattern and the tuck setting. I've started my stitch pattern and you can see that these needles have tucked and there are strands over the held needles.

Now take the flat edge of your needle pusher and push those needles back into middle position. Use the 2x2 needle pusher again and push the opposite needles to hold. Make sure you are not holding the edge stitches. Knit across and notice the strands now over those needles.

Repeat this for the pattern hold sets of two needles, knit across, alternate the sets of needles and tuck. Making sure you aren't tucking the end needles. Remember this is tuck and tuck requires more weight than stockinette.

Be sure to watch your knitting to make sure that the stitches are knitting off correctly. I encourage you to to give this one a try for yourself. It's a little hard to see in the photos but it has great texture and the purl side is quite attractive and textured as well.
I hope you'll give it a try.

Whether you are hand-manipulating and reforming stitches or knitting 1x1 ribbing with the ribber, plan ahead for perfectly matched seams. Having an uninterrupted seam is the goal. As you're setting up your knitting, each edge will be a bit different.

When knitting with a ribber, make sure that one edge, (let's say the left side) has two needles on the ribber and the opposite side of the knitted piece will have one needle on the ribber. This will form purl stitches on the edges with a 1x1 needle arrangement in between.

For your second piece, place two needles on the right side on the ribber and one needle on the opposite or the left side on the ribber. This is what the two pieces would look like next to each other, as if you were looking at them from the private side.

You'll see two purl stitches on one edge and one purl stitch on the other. When seaming, use a full stitch mattress stitch and the 1x1 sequence is uninterrupted. Now when you're hand-manipulating the same holds true if you're reforming for 1x1 ribbing.

Always remember you don't want to reform those edge stitches so they remain purl stitches as viewed from the private side that's facing you on the knitting machine. The trick is to leave two stitches plain on one side of the knitting and when the edges are joined, you'll get the desired results.

Maybe a bit of a brain twister at first. Right side, wrong side, private and public sides. But the bottom line is you want to end up with two purl stitches on one edge of a piece and one purl stitch on the other edge that's going to join.
Take time to plan this ahead for beautiful 1x1 ribbed seams.

Let's take a moment to review slip. Using the slip setting of your machine, needles in B or working position will not knit. This is used for the slip stitch technique and knitting in the round with the ribber. It's also referred to as free pass.

Let's say you need to move your carriage from one side of the bed to the other without knitting or dropping stitches. Keep all needles in B. Set your carriage to slip and you can safely pass it across the knitting. On some knitting machines, you can set the cam to slip, left, right or both.

With the Taitexma 160, there is only one part lever. Engaging that part lever means needles in working or B position will slip in both directions. To knit I-cord or anytime you want to alternate slipping and knitting you need to move the lever.

With the part lever engaged, I'm pushing my carriage right and the needles slip. You can see that the stitches didn't knit and the yarn is just carried across. Move the lever to plain and it will cancel the slip and knit the stitches when I knit back.

We create I-cord by alternating slip and knit with the passing of the carriage. This can get really tedious on this machine if you're flipping that lever back and forth. But there is an easier way. One more time. With the part lever engaged, needles in B will slip.

But needles in D or E will knit. So to knit I-cord, put three or four needles into working or B position, pass the carriage left and the needles will slip. Pull out the needles to D or E position, pass the carriage and then stitches will knit and they're all returned to B position.

With the needles in B pass that carriage left and the needles slip. Pull the needles out and the stitches will knit and they'll automatically be put back into B position. This is so much easier. No need to flip that part lever back and forth.

Here's an example of free pass. My carriage is set to slip, the cam lever is set to part. When I pull out needles, they will knit even though part is engaged. With the needles remaining in B position, I can free pass back and the stitches won't knit or drop.

Watch as I knit my RTR hat. Now, I know it's a funny name, but you'll quickly see why it's named RTR. Use this watch cap as inspiration for your next hat. It has a reverse stockinette Hung hem, a couple of reverse stockinette amd 1x1 rib inserts it's a 4 gore cap and it's gathered at the top, allowing for a ponytail.

When you build your pattern, be sure to account for negative ease. My mannequin's head is 22 inches, so I built my pattern to a finished size of 20 inches. Before I started knitting, I also sketched out my texture stripes.

The body of my hat, the H dimension in my pattern was 43 rows, so I decided that each of my stripes would be six rows alternating stockinette, reverse stockinette and hand manipulated 1x1 ribbing. Start by casting on with waste yarn and ravel cord.

I knit for about an inch and a half. Then I turned the tension to the loosest setting (the largest number) and I also released the yarn from the tension wire and held the working yarn by hand and knit one row. This created a really loose turning row.

For the second half I knit the same number of rows for the hem. For more tips about hems, especially one of my favorites of picot hem, please visit the Knit It Now classroom "Hem and Edges". To create a hem with the purl side showing, remove, turn and rehang the hem.

Now, I don't have a garter bar for this machine, so I used a circular hand knitting needle to remove the stitches. I turned the work so that the knit side was facing me and then rehung each of the stitches back in the needles.

Once the stitches were hung back on the machine, I picked up the open cast on stitches to hang the hem. I then immediately knit my first stripe, which is stockinette in contrast to the reverse stockinette hem. I continued to follow my plan, and I alternated RTR and hand-reformed one by one sections to finish this "H" part of my hat.

At this gauge, re-forming these stitches wasn't too tedious, and I really like the texture. So planning the public side of my knitting, I started to shape the wedges. After dividing the number of stitches according to my pattern, I scrapped off each section.

To scrap off with my working yarn at the right, I pulled all the needles to hold and set my carriage to holding the working yarn. I was then able to free pass over to the left side of my knitting. I put the first group of needles into work and then just scrapped off those needles.

I put the second group of needles in work and scrapped them off and repeated for the third group of needles. Then free pass to the right to get the carriage back to the side with the working yarn so I can continue knitting that first wedge.

Now I'm ready to start shaping the wedge according to my pattern. I'm decreasing one stitch on each side every row. Notice that I'm decreasing two stitches in from the edge, and I'm working a two-step decrease. For more shaping tips, visit Knit it Now shaping tutorials.

I want to leave an opening for a ponytail. So instead of decreasing down to one or two stitches, as the pattern tells me, I only decreased down to eight stitches on each wedge a little over one inch. I then created eyelets in each wedge to create holes so I could cinch up the top of the hat with I-cord.

If you haven't yet knit I-cord, check the Knit It Now Classroom I-cord on the machine. It's easy. After transferring stitches for the eyelets, I continued to knit for about an inch, and then I bound off each of the wedges using the I-cord.
The hat can be gathered closed, or the opening can accommodate a ponytail or a messy bun.

If you find your stitch symbols palette, empty it's because somehow the font file that displays the symbols on the screen has gotten erased or corrupted on your computer. There's an easy fix. Go from this to this. First, download this file to a folder on your computer where it will be easy to to find.

You can just stick it on your desktop if you'd like. Once it's installed, you can erase it from your desktop. 2. Go to your Windows search box and type FONTS. 3. A listing of the fonts on your machine will display. 4. Drag the file that you downloaded and drop it into that fonts folder.
5. Close DesignaKnit and any other Windows you have open and restart your computer. When you open DesignaKnit, the fonts will be correctly displayed and you'll be good to go.

You've found a sweater pattern that you love. The neckline, design, and stitch pattern are just perfect, but it's sleeveless. Now, I don't know about you, but I'm past the point of wanting to show off my arms and I need sleeves.

If the pattern is a drop shoulder or basic square armhole, you can easily add sleeves with the Knit It Now custom sleeves tool. Measure both your front and back armholes from the pattern diagram or instructions. Determine your desired sleeve length, short sleeve, three quarter or full length, and be sure to adjust the wrist or arm measurement accordingly.
Choosing your custom sleeve pattern instructions, choose to pick up and knit the sleeves from the top down or start at the cuff and knit up. No more bare arms. Make the sweater your own.

Stitch pattern using DesignaKnit with your machine is accomplished by sending data from your computer to the carriage, instructing the carriage to select and position needles. Before you fast forward, please hang in there with me for just a moment.

It's important that you understand this. In general, stitch patterning is accomplished by the position of the needles and how they pass through the channels under the carriage. The channels are controlled by the cam lever.

The red line in this image indicates the path that the needle butts take. Notice how the levers change the configuration of the channel, therefore, the path the needle butts travel. As the needle butts are directed through the channel, the needles are positioned to form stitches.

Each needle will either knit, slip, tuck, or knit with a different yarn. Please remove your carriage, turn it over, hold it securely, shift the cam lever, and observe what happens. In the following exercises, we will explore the different stitch patterns available on your machine and the steps for accomplishing them.

But remember, it's DesignaKnit, sending signals to the carriage that determines which needles pass through the path under the carriage, and it's the cam lever that determines the configuration of the path and which stitch type is formed.

Threading the carriage for plating can be a bit tricky on this machine. Just remember that the point is to have two yarns in the number one yarn feeder positioned so they remain separate as you're knitting. Looking very closely at the yarn feeder, there are two openings that will be used for the plating.

The goal is to have one yarn in the regular opening and the contrasting yarn in that back slot. The easiest way I found to thread that back opening is to use a double- eye needle or a darning needle. Thread the needle with your yarn and slip it down through that back slot.

The manual suggests pushing a latch tool up from underneath the carriage and using the hook to catch the yarn, and then pull the yarn down to thread it in the feeder. Using a work hook from a ribber works too. Whichever method you use, make sure that the two yarns are in separate feeders.
They move smoothly and they're not hung up anywhere. Now, with the yarns positioned this way, I can knit my plating. One yarn will be positioned in front of the other.

This beautiful tuck lace stitch pattern is a very simple example of what we can knit by combining tuck and needles out of work. It's created by putting needles out of work on each side of the tuck stitches. The Stitch World books and some vintage publications may show the stitch pattern in a diagram that looks like this.

But on the needle bed, how do you know what needles to put out of work? The easiest thing is to do a test run. Use some scrap yarn and cast on enough needles for a few repeats of the stitch pattern. Cast on over every needle and knit a couple of rows.

Then engage your punch card or electronics and set your machine to tuck. Knit across all the needles in tuck and observe what happens. You can see which stitches are being tucked. With this stitch pattern, needles are out of work on each side of the tucked stitches.

You could transfer or empty these needles and continue to test your stitch pattern in your scrap yarn, or just note which needles need to be out of work when you cast on with your garment yarn. Using a test run ensures that you put the correct needles out of work according to your pattern.

of what I consider to be the worst cast on ever. I understand that with a lace carriage, I can't pull needles out past the B position. Most of the closed cast on methods that I use pull the needles out further. But this sloppy, open cast on is often taught to new knitters.
