No wonder they get discouraged. Here are the steps. I'm demonstrating this on a Silver Reed machine with my lace carriage, but this method is often recommended on other machines with gate pegs. I have my lace carriage in place and it's set for plain knitting.

Align all the needles to B position and then thread up the carriage. Knit across. You'll see open loops across all the needles. Next, run a strand of ravel cord behind the gate pegs and in front of the needle hooks. The object here is to hold those loose loops down with the ravel cord.

Hold the tail of the working yarn and the tails of the ravel cord securely. Pass the carriage and knit one row. If all the stitches knit correctly, continue knitting four or five rows. Release the knitting by slipping the ravel cord out.

Immediately, you see a problem when I hang weights on the edge stitches. The stitches are not secure. As a matter of fact, the stitches will ravel, and because of all those open stitches, the edge of your knitting is going to be a mess.

I have never understood why anyone would recommend or use this method. Why not simply work a nice closed cast on with your regular knitting carriage, and then switch to the lace carriage? If you don't have more than one cast on method in your bag of tricks, I suggest you learn at least two or three to use for different situations.
But please stay away from this worst cast on ever.

With certain stitch patterns like tuck and lace, they require even weight across your knitting. One way to achieve this is to use a ribber cast on comb. Now, even if you don't have a ribber attached, the comb can come in handy.

On a single bed, put every other needle into work, leaving the other needles in out of work position. Knit across, forming loops. Carefully push that cast on comb into the loops that are formed. Insert the wire in the comb.

Now, be careful to keep that comb and the wire in front of the gate pegs and pull down. The knitting should look like this. Keeping the comb out of the way of the carriage, knit across. Then put all the needles into work and knit a few rows.
Hang some ribber weights as needed. With this scrap in place, you can now knit a row of ravel cord and work a closed cast on to continue your knitting.

Is a nifty little device that was created specifically for the Singer/ Studio SK 150 and SK 151 bulky machines. It's a 12 stitch repeat pattern selector to make quick work of using punch cards on a manual machine without a built in punch card mechanism.

If you are lucky enough to find one of these rare devices, it could also work for any 9 millimeter bulky machine. It consists of the pattern selector device, a needle selector, card snaps, punch cards, and it originally came with a unique number strip for the needle bed that was marked for sets of 12 repeats of the needles.

As long as you have these pieces, you can use this without the number strip. The pattern selector has slots that are designed to fit over the screw heads on a Silver machine. I'm not showing an SK-150 here, but the screw heads happen to be the same and I can mount the device on the machine.

The device slips over the screw heads. There's no need to adjust them. The original punch cards were fairly long, long enough to go through the device so the ends could be snapped together and the card made into a loop for continuous knitting.

With the printed side down, feed one end of the card into the lower part of the slot. Once it's moved a few inches through, loop the card and feed the other end into the upper slot until it catches. Then carefully turn the knob, advancing the end of the card that is in the upper slot.

Keep turning until you can join the two ends into a loop. Line up the ends and join them with the card snaps. I'm using a long piece of blank cardstock as an example. I don't have the original cards. Once the loop is formed, position the card to look like this.

Now, be careful. I discovered that the Toyota 12 stitch repeat cards do not fit in this device. The holes are not positioned to the same and they will not work. Be sure you have Studio/ Singer 12 stitch cards. Be sure the cards overlap correctly so they don't jam as you cycle it through the device.

Position the stitch pattern so the row you want to knit is on top. Push the reset button so the fingers of the needle selector are aligned. Then with the A side of the needle selector facing you, push the fingers into the pattern slot to select needles.

Rise the needle pusher and notice how some of the fingers are in out of work position. Using the working fingers as you would any other needle selector, pull needles out to D position. Repeat this across the row for your stitch pattern.

This is where the special number strip would come in handy, making it easier to see groups of 12 needles. When all the needles have been selected and the carriage is set for patterning, knit across the row. For the next pattern row, push the reset button again and advance the card.

Repeat selecting the fingers of the needle selector and selecting the new needles across the row. Remember, this device is completely manual. You need to reset the needle pusher, advance the card, and reselect the fingers of the needle pusher for each row.
Even though this is a manual device, it can make selecting needles a whole lot easier and faster with these machines.

To replace a number strip, start by completely removing the sponge bar or the presser bar. This is my ribber, but the main bed is done the same way. Slip the old number strip out. Prepare the new strip by putting a bit of oil on your fingertip and spread a thin amount on the backside of the strip.
This will help keep it in place. Slide the new strip in place and align it with the needles. Replace the sponge bar. And happy knitting.

This pretty and useful braid is easy to knit on the machine. Use tuck stitch for texture over a few stitches. Cast on an odd number of stitches and knit a few rows and hang some weight. Set your carriage to hold. If you're not familiar with the hold setting on your machine, check your manual and watch the video at knititnow.

Com/HOLD. Pull the center needle all the way out. Knit four to 6 rows, holding that center needle. Notice how loops are formed over the held needle. Cancel hold and knit two rows. Continue this sequence for the desired length of your braid.

Depending on your machine and your chosen yarn, you are limited to the number of rows you can hold. Those loops stack up and may be difficult to knit. You may need to add extra weight with your fingers or claw weights so the stitches knit off correctly.

Try different row counts and see what works for you. Here is a pretty variation. In this example, I cast on nine needles and held two stitches for six rows. This makes a wider braid with a pretty scalloped edge. Both sides are interesting.

Here's a five stitch braid on a standard gauge machine. Holding with the Russell levers on a Silver Reed machine creates manual tuck stitch for the texture of this braid. No matter what machine you use, I hope you'll play with the technique to create a fancy braid of your own.

Many machine knitters complain about their stash. "I have so much yarn, I'll never use it in this lifetime." Well, put it to use. There are people out there who could use knitted items that you can make. Dust off that machine, use up that yarn, and get a feeling of satisfaction for making something for someone who's in need.

Plan on learning techniques and practicing the skills that you need to improve your knitting. Here are six ways that you can knit for charity and help others. Knitting blankets or lap robes is a wonderful way to provide warmth and comfort to those in need.

Think about preemies and newborns, the elderly, those undergoing chemo, or homeless shelters. Animal shelters also provide blankets for our furry friends. Consider washable, soft yarns for blankets. But the sky's the limit in using color and stitch patterns.

A really easy blanket is our Right Angles Blanket. This is a great exercise in learning about gauge. Knit a swatch and let our pattern determine the stitches and rows for your blanket size. We even include a tool to help you determine if you have enough yarn for the size you've chosen.

Knit four to six squares, attach them together (as you knit) for minimal finishing. Susanna's Blanket adds the challenge of short row shaping for its interesting design. It's a fun one to knit, especially in self-striping yarns.

Knitted hats are always in demand, especially during the colder months. You can donate them to homeless shelters, hospitals, or organizations that support cancer patients. Or you can knit for premature babies. Experiment with different patterns and yarns to create a variety of styles.

Hats can just be plain old rectangles, easy to knit. With our Mile-a-Minute Hat project, you cast on one time and you can knit a handful of hats in one knitting session. Once they're off the machine, seam up and finish the hat in front of the TV or out on the deck.

Maybe you'll challenge yourself to shape the top of a hat for great fit. Dust off your ribber and knit some hats in the round. Any hat with a fold up brim will fit almost anyone, and the doubled brim makes for warmer ears.

If you are in the US, let me remind you of Linda Williams' hat contest at Country Knitting of Maine. Another quick and easy and useful project are soap sacks. These are washcloth pouches that can be practical to donate and a thoughtful gift.

They hold bars of soap and double as exfoliating washcloths. Donate them to homeless shelters or organizations that offer hygiene items to those in need. Stacey at soapsacks. Com inspired me to put all those bits and pieces of cotton yarn to good use.

Plus I've had so much fun knitting a simple 4 inch by 6 inch project, knowing that I'm helping someone in need. How about some more rectangles? Scarfs and shawls can provide warmth and comfort. Consider knitting various lengths, colors, and stitch patterns.

Donate them to homeless shelters, women's shelters, or organizations that support people facing cold weather. I've discovered that when my neck is warm, I'm warm. Maybe a needy person's coat or jacket isn't very warm. A scarf can add extra comfort in cold weather, and you can help them stay warm.

If you've graduated past a plain old rectangle, consider our butterfly shawl. The shaping is easy and it adds a bit of interest to the knitting and to the finished shawl. Here's another reason to dust off that ribber or garter carriage.

Play with stitch patterns and sizes and use our Rectangle Square tool to calculate how many stitches to cast on and how many rows to knit. Use our Yarn Calculator to determine if you have enough yarn to knit the size you've chosen.

Are you ready for a challenge? How about mittens? Handknitted mittens are welcome during the winter. Choose soft and insulating yarns to keep hands cozy. Look for organizations that collect winter accessories for children or the homeless.

Our mitten collection has five styles and eight customizable sizes. You can create easy to knit, comfortable mittens. Are you feeling extra ambitious? Maybe you're looking to learn or practice some new-to-you techniques. Use up that yarn with our easiest and fastest sweater pattern the Kid's Squirrel Cardigan.

If you can cast on and bind off, then you can knit this. It's knit in one piece with just two side seams. Another one-piece quickie is our two hour child and infant cardigan. This one gives you good short row practice and can be finished in no time.

Don't be afraid to knit sweaters. Will they be perfect? Probably not. Will they be judged at the county fair? No. The recipient will be happy to have something warm to slip on that was made with love. I encourage you to use up that yarn, put your machine to use, and knit for charity.
You'll feel great helping others. Happy knitting.

Which needles should be out of work? By default, knitting machines position stitch patterns in the center of the needle bed. Electronic machines allow us to move the position of stitch patterns on the needle bed. But for this conversation, we're looking at stitch patterns being centered on the needle bed.

There are a number of ways to determine what needles need to be out of work. First, study the pattern. Many of our pattern books, like the Stitch World books, will display stitch diagrams with the needle out of work looking like this.

Keep in mind that the pattern is centered on the needle bed, so draw a line down the center of the diagram and the O indicates needles out of work. If there are an odd number of stitches in the stitch multiple, put the extra stitch on the left.

In this example, needles number left 3 and right 2 will be out of work. Number 2, study the punch card. This time draw a line down the center of the punch card and look for holes and no holes. Remember, holes mean needles are knitting and no holes are stitches that are going to be tucked.

Now, we don't want to tuck two stitches side by side. So in this example, there are full columns of no holes, which indicate that these should be needles out of work. Put the needles out of work and these stitches will tuck next to those needles out of work.

In this example, there are columns of holes. And what if you put these needles out of work and let these stitches tuck? Number three, the best way to determine needle positions is by testing the stitch pattern. On Brother machine's preselect needles, so we can do a dry run without yarn to establish what needles will be tucking.

In this example, we can see that needle number one right is tucking for two rows, and then needle number one left is tucking for two rows. According to our diagram, we want needles out of work next to the needles that are tucking.

There'll be two needles out of work. So I'll set up my needle bed, two needles out of work, two needles in, two needles out, two needles in. On Silver's, singer, studio machines, we can test by knitting a little bit of tuck and observing which needles are tucking.

We'll cast on with some waste yarn and knit a few rows, then engage the punch card or electronics and knit across the first row, noting which needles tuck, knit a few more rows, watching the tuck sequence, and note which needles are tucking.

Now, for this stitch pattern, we want needles out of work next to the tuck stitches. Now that we've identified the tuck needles, we can put the correct needles out of work. With the needles arranged correctly, you can now test knit that tuck lace with your scrap yarn.

Here's a tip. Take a photo of your needle bed to record the needle arrangement and keep it with your punch card or keep a record for the next time you want to use this stitch pattern. For manual machines, you'll follow a stitch diagram.

I suggest creating a cheat sheet to follow to know when to manually put needles in hold for the tuck stitches. If you use DesignaKnit, use the interactive knitting feature to identify the position of the needles out of work.

Here's a tip. No matter what machine you're using, if you create your stitch pattern in DesignaKnit, choosing the knitting method right side facing or wrong side facing impacts how the stitch pattern is positioned on the needle bed.
So be aware of this if you don't use Interactive Knitting and you use DesignaKnit to create punch cards.

I am planning a hat with a doubled band of 2x2 ribbing. Here's a trick to create a turning row for a more defined, sharp fold in the band. Here's that band just folded over. For my turning row, I transferred the stitches. Main bed to ribber, ribber to main bed.

The knitting now has a crisp fold and lays flat. You could use this for cuffs or anywhere you're going to be doubling your ribbing. Try it with other needle arrangements, and I'm sure you'll be pleasantly surprised.

This lacy stitch pattern is an easy one to work and remember, with no cheat sheet needed. Cast on a multiple of five stitches plus two. For my scarf, I cast on 25 stitches plus two for the edge. To keep the edges neat. There are two needles and work on each side with no transfers over these needles.

I started by knitting two rows and ended with the carriage on the right. That's not critical, but be consistent for your entire scarf. The stitch pattern consists of transferring stitches to a center needle. First, transfer to the right, knit two rows, and then transfer to the left and knit two rows.

Alternating the transfers creates the lace. To make things easier, I marked my needle bed with a dry erase pen. You can also use a pencil. This made it a no-brainer as to which needles were the center needles each time. after you work your transfers, make sure the empty needles are in working position before you knit the next row.

Do this on every transfer row. Now don't get lost if you need to take a break. Either keep track of your row counter, for example, transfer right on row two, transfer left on row four, right on row six, left on row eight, or read your knitting.

This is my center stitch. Looking below, I can see the large eyelet from the previous transfer. This tells me that I'm transferring right on this row. That's it. A pretty and easy stitch pattern with beautiful results. When you've knit your required number of rows or you're running out of yarn, knit two rows plain and bind off loosely.
Block your scarf and enjoy. Happy knitting.

The Silver Reed YC6 Yarn Changer is designed to be used for both single and double bed knitting. In comparison, for Brother machines, there are separate color changers for single and double bed. Just so you don't get confused as I'm recording this, I may use the term color changer and yarn changer alternately.

I mean the same thing. Start by tilting the bed by using the ribber clamps. Even if you're going to be using the color changer for single bed knitting, you need to tilt the bed so the device fits in place. Once the bed is secure with the ribber clamps, make room for the color changer by pushing the sponge bar to the right.

It'll protrude 2 to 3 CM on the right side, and it'll remain in this position as long as the color changer is in place. Loosen the setting wheel until it stops. This is releasing the setting plate that will be inserted into the needle bed where the sponge bar normally lives.

Insert that setting plate and wiggle it around until it seats. At the same time, push the color changer towards the right until the edge of that yarn changer sits firmly against the end of the bed. Push the release button to align all the holder buttons to the "O" position.

When I got my color changer, this holder was all the way out. I gently pulled it out a little more, felt a click, and then released it. The spring brought it back into position. By pushing the release button, it aligned that holder with the others.

In this position, all the holders are out of work. Again, because this color changer can be used in two ways, we need to align it into its correct position for how we're knitting. For single bed knitting, loosen the change screw and push the arm up, and then tighten the screw.

For double bed knitting, loosen the change screw and let the arm drop. Then tighten that screw again to secure the changer arm. Next, we'll set up the tension mast. Snap the tension guide onto the yarn rod or the yarn mast and slide it down to secure it so it doesn't twist around.

Carefully pull up the tension spring of the tensioner assembly and snap it into position. Insert the yarn rod or that mast into the front slot of the tensioner. It insert the lower end of the yarn rod or mast into the slot in the needle bed and rotate it so it's secure and doesn't twist.
Next, exchange the knitter connecting sinker plate with the yarn changer arm and you're ready to start using your yarn changer.

Here is an extra fast, closed cast-on. Now, it may not be the prettiest cast-on you can find, but it is closed and it will get your knitting started quickly. It uses slip. I'm showing it on a Brother machine using the part buttons.

On Silver/Singer machines, set the side levers to slip and you'll get the same results. Put into work the number of needles needed and then pull every other needle all the way out. Let's call these the even number needles.

Set your carriage to slip. On my Brother machine, I engaged both part buttons. Knit across. Notice that the needles that you pulled have loops and the needles that remained in working position slipped. The yarn passed under those needles.

Next, pull those slipped needles all the way out. Let's call these the odd needles, with the carriage still set to slip, knit across. This time, the odd needles will have a loop and the even needles form a loose, somewhat sloppy stitch.

We'll do this again. Pull the original, even needles all the way out. Pass the carriage. Again, the odd needles will slip. Finally, pull the odd needles out. When you knit, those odd needles will form sloppy stitches and the even needles slip.

Continue knitting, and you'll see that you have a nice closed cast-on that won't run, but you did it in very few steps. If you struggle with this, consider using a cast-on comb on that first row. It may help form the stitches more cleanly.

Before you get started connecting your ribber, turn it over and locate the slot for the racking handle and insert the racking handle. It's easier to visualize at this point. Later, you can insert and remove the handle with the ribber attached.

In the manual, this is called an auxiliary piece. It's also known as a setting plate, and it holds the ribber joiner in place to join the ribber to the main bed. Slip the setting plate into the main bed slot as shown. There's a right and left auxiliary piece or setting plate.

And finger-tighten the nut, leaving it loose. Repeat for the other side. Pick up the ribber and carefully insert the joiner into the auxiliary piece or the setting plate. You'll be inserting both sides at the same time, so it might be helpful to have an extra set of hands available.

Once the ribber is in place, tighten the screws in the setting plate. Position the ribber joiner support leg against your table and secure it with a clamp. Repeat this for the other side. Next, rotate the pushup cam in the direction of the arrow and be sure that it clicks into place.

This provides extra support for the ribber. Using both hands, raise the ribber all the way up and confirm that the connections are tight. Next, you'll join the knitting carriages and explore using your ribber.

Let's take a closer look at shoulder seams when working cut and sew. In this sample, I've knit a back and two cardigan fronts. I scrapped off the shoulders. Each has 20 stitches, and I scrapped off the neck openings separately.

Now, for this sample, I then used a template to mark the neck openings, but this is a case of "do as I say, not as I did." What I should have done was join the shoulders, then marked the neck opening. Either way, you can see my shoulder join with the waste yarn removed.

The marks and the upcoming stitch lines are carefully positioned away from that shoulder seam. I left my orange neck opening waste yarn in place. You could also choose to bind off the neck openings, but this whole area is going to be cut away and the raw edges will be enclosed with my band.

Here is the single line of straight stitches. Notice that I did not sew those shoulder seam stitches. Then a line or two of zig -zag should be enough to secure my stitches. Notice that I didn't stitch along those shoulder stitches.

When using a serger, you have to be extra careful not to stitch those shoulder stitches. The secret here is to isolate those shoulder stitches when stitching and cutting the neckline. Now, it's difficult to see in this photo, but when hanging the neck edge on the machine to form the band, care needs to be taken to secure those shoulder stitches.

Even though we stretch the neckline when hanging it on the machine for a neat finish, don't stretch in that shoulder seam area. Once you finish the band, the neck edge should be neat and tidy along those secure shoulder seams.

Let's knit a test collar with a sandwich band that can be used to cover a cut and sew edge. This could also be used to attach a collar to a shaped neckline. Now, this is not a beginner project. There are a number of steps to construct this collar, and there are also a number of skills you must master or review before attempting it.

The first one is a neat full needle, rib cast on. The cast on edge of your collar will be the focus of your garment, so be sure you practice and knit a cast on that you like. I used the broken toe cast on. It starts with three slip rows.

Number two, be familiar with knitting and full needle rib. Remember, because all needles are on work, you'll need a thinner yarn than you might normally knit with on your machine. Number three, you must be familiar with setting your machine for tubular knitting.

We will knit in the round for the pocket or that sandwich section of this project. Plus, we will scrap off the ribber stitches, leaving the main bed stitches in work. You also need to be comfortable with manually pulling stitches through the knitting.

Now, this can get tricky, so remove any distractions, get a good night's sleep, and focus. You also need to be comfortable with binding off in the stitch-by-stitch method with long loops. Of course, you could scrap off and hand-knit to secure the last stitches.

Now, if you're feeling comfortable with all of these skills, let's get started. Instead of creating a cut and sew neckline for our test. I'm just using a surged edge of a swatch. It isn't even the same yarn as my collar. No matter, we just want to practice the steps.

First, determine how many needles you'll need for your collar. Hold the edge up against the machine, stretching it slightly. Set your machine for full needle rib. Half pitch, and put the required number of needles in work on both beds.

Cast on with the method of your choice. I'm working a broken toe cast on, which will give me a strand to tighten so that I can steam and set that cast on edge. Now, if you aren't familiar with this cast on, I suggest you give it a try.

Next, measure a collar on a sweater or a shirt to determine the length you like. Remember, it's going to fold over, so you might want to make it a little bit longer. This is a good time to experiment. Knit the desired length of your collar.

Set your machine for circular knitting. For example, slip to the left on the main bed, slip to the right on the ribber, and knit about a half inch worth of rows. Remember, it takes two passes of the carriage to complete a row in tubular knitting.

I knit a total of six rows, 12 passes of the carriage. We'll scrap off the ribber stitches only by canceling slip on the ribber and setting your main bed to slip in both directions. Remove the main yarn from the yarn feeder and thread the carriage with scrap yarn.

Knit 4-6 rows of scrap on the ribber only. Notice that the stitches are going to bunch up a little bit, so don't knit too many rows and make your scrap a good contrasting color. When you're done there, after knitting just a few rows, drop those stitches and drop your ribber.

Notice the pocket that's been created. Next, we'll attach the garment edge. With the right side facing up, position the garment edge across the main bed. The cut edge of your neckline will be facing you. Press that cut edge against the sinker post to position the cut edge inside that pocket or sandwich.

Push the main bed needles through the neck edge, and re-hang the scrapped-off pocket stitches from the ribber and position them in the hooks of the needles. Make sure you close all of the laches and carefully pull the stitches through both the neck edge and the stitches that are remaining on that main bed.

I removed the waist yarn to confirm that I picked up all of my stitches. Oops, I missed one. You must take care with the laches so they don't catch on the knitting and the stitches remain in the hooks of the needles. This can be a little tedious.

Take your time. Flip the garment towards you and carefully pop the knitting off the gate pegs. Handknit a loose row with fairly long loops. I just hand-knit some large loops and then pulled loop through loop to bind off. Now, if you prefer not to have such a visible bind off, you could sew those stitches in place.

With all the steps involved, you can see how things can get a bit confusing and easily go wrong. Before trying this technique on a garment, I suggest you knit at least one other test collar using the edge of a swatch, or maybe get brave and use a sample cut and sew neckline.

With a good mental picture, I'm sure you will have success. First, we knit the collar, leaving it on the machine. Then we knit in the round to create the sandwich pocket. We then positioned the cut edge in that sandwich and pushed the needles through the cut edge.
We pulled one-half of the sandwich stitches through that cut edge and neatly bound off. Have fun knitting your sandwich collar.

This variation of English rib produces a wide, thick, textured fabric that doesn't have a lot of stretch. It has the racked texture on one side and what appears to be one by one ribbing on the other. It's based on English rib.

Now, English rib is basically ribbing in a one by one needle arrangement, tucking every other row on one bed. The tucking can be set up either on the main bed or the ribber. If you haven't worked English rib, please watch this video at knititnow.

Com/englishrib. It has tips and tricks for success with this stitch pattern. Once you're comfortable with English rib, try adding some racking to produce swung English rib. It can be worked by tucking right or left on either the main bed or the ribber.

No matter which variation you choose to form this stitch pattern, you'll be swinging the ribber with the racking handle and distorting the stitches. Start by casting on for one-by-one ribbing with the method of your choice end with the carriage on your right and the ribber set to P5 and knit a few rows.

Be sure you have the outside needles on the main bed in work. The needle arrangement should start like this. Now, before starting to knit, let's take a look at our end needles. We'll be racking to seven, so looking closely, I can see that I need to pull another needle into work on the ribber to fill this gap.

Starting with the one-by-one needle set up, racked to five, I'll set my main bed to tuck in one direction. For this brother machine, I'm pushing in the right tuck button. On a silver machine, you'll set your cam to tuck and your right side lever to tuck.

I'll knit to the left and both beds knit. Knit to the right and the main bed has loops over each of the needles. But wait. To keep our edges neat and to prevent dropped stitches, we don't want to tuck those end needles. So every time the carriage will be tucking, in this example, when the carriage passes right, I'll pull the end needles all the way out, and they'll knit while the rest of the needles tuck.

So the first sequence is rack to five, knit left, all needles will knit, pull the end needles out on that main bed, knit right, and all of the needles on the main bed will tuck, except for those end needles. The second sequence is rack to seven and then knit left.

All needles will knit. Pull the end needles out, knit right, and all but the end needles will tuck. Repeat sequence one and two for the stitch pattern. So knit a few inches and then stop. Notice that my edges are neat and tidy with no dropped stitches and these edges will easily be seamed or they'll stand neatly on their own.

You want to experiment a little bit? Try tucking in the opposite direction and continue knit for a few inches. Sequence one, we'll tuck left and knit right, and then rack. Sequence two, again, we'll tuck left and knit right.

When you drop the work from the machine, by tucking on the main bed, you'll see that the stitch pattern is showing on the side away from you. If you'd prefer to have the stitch pattern showing on the side towards you, set your ribber to tuck.
Do sequence one and sequence two tucking on the ribber. Be sure to pull those end needles out and align that end those end needles as you need to.

Here's an interesting stitch pattern that I'm calling Connect the Dots. It's worked with short rows, and it isn't hard to knit, but it takes a bit of planning and concentration. Let's figure this out by knitting a single repeat.

Looking at the diagram, notice that the dot is worked over nine stitches outlined in red. It'll be knit using partial knitting, and these five rows in the diagram represent a single row in the knitted piece. The gray boxes in the diagram are needles that are held out of work.

The curved symbols remind us to wrap and prevent holes when changing directions. To practice knitting one repeat of the dots, start by casting on 19 stitches with the main color. Knit 6 to 8 rows and end with the carriage on the right.

Remove the main color from the carriage and set it aside. Set your carriage to hold so that any needles in the D or E position will not knit. Opposite the carriage, pull five needles to hold. Thread the carriage with the contrasting color and knit across 14 stitches.

Be sure the edge stitches knit completely and wrap that first needle. Opposite the carriage, put five needles plus two more in hold. Knit to the right and confirm all the stitches knit correctly. Don't forget to wrap. Opposite the carriage again, put two more needles in hold, knit left, and wrap.

Opposite the carriage one last time, put two more needles in hold, knit right, and wrap. This completes the partial knitting for the dot. Now put five needles plus two in work and knit left. Break the contrasting color yarn and remove it from the carriage.

Now put all needles in hold position. With the carriage remaining in hold, free pass to the right and pick up the main color yarn. Now cancel the hold setting. Thread the carriage with the main yarn and knit eight rows. You can bind off or just drop the knitting from the machine.

For an all-over design, we'll repeat this sequence across the row and then knit a few main color rows and repeat the dots again, alternating the position of the dots. Have fun knitting your connect the dots stitch pattern.

This beautiful knit weave stitch pattern combines automatic patterning to form the knit weave floats along with picking up the long floats manually for graphic appeal. The DesignaKnit stitch pattern looks like this. The weave over symbol selects needles and the weaving yarn passes over those needles.

However, DesignaKnit does not have a symbol for picking up those long floats. We will Follow this diagram for picking up the floats. Looking at the punch card, the black squares or the holes indicate the weaving floats. The white squares are stitches that knit.

Let's walk through the 16 row repeat for this stitch pattern. I'm using a Brother machine, so the needles are pre-selecting. But with Singer, Silver, Studio, and other machines, follow your manual for knit weave and pick up the floats as shown in the diagram.

The first pass of my carriage sets up the first row. I like to manually lay the weaving yarn over the selected needles, but you can use the knit weave method of your choice. When I knit across my first row, notice there are seven stitches between the selected needles and There's a long float between those needles.

The second row of the pattern is the same, creating another seven-stitch float. Now on my Brother machine, I can see that there are no needles selected for the next row. It will knit plain. Keeping the weaving yarn out of the way, according to the pattern, I'll just knit two rows.

The pattern has preselected groups of three needles. Before I weave the next row, however, I'll pick up both of those large floats from below and hang them on the center of a group of three. I'll do this across the row. Then, according to the pattern, I'll weave the next four rows.

Notice the shorter floats. The next sequence of two rows creates long floats. Notice that the long floats are alternating in position from the first group of long floats. When these two rows are complete, I'll knit two plain rows.

Groups of three needles are selected. Before knitting the next section, pick up the long floats and hang them on the center needle of the groups of three, just like before. Knit four rows of short floats again. And repeat the sequence starting with two rows of long floats.

Here's my booboo. As I was working this stitch pattern, I caught myself passing my carriage too far from the edge of the knitting, forming loops on edges. This is something to watch for any time you're knitting. In this case, I was more worried about positioning that weaving yarn and lost focus about how far I was passing my carriage.

In a previous video, we walked through the steps for creating a single dot. Let's go one step further and explore adding rows of dots. First, let's think of this stitch pattern as a series of units. In this example, each unit consists of a single row plus a dot in contrasting color.

The contrasting color is represented by both light and dark blue in this diagram. Gray are stitches that are not knit. Remember, we're working short rows and partial knitting. And white in this diagram is the main color. This entire gray section represents a single row of knitting.

The dots are seven stitches, an odd number, and there are eleven stitches, an odd number between the dots. The rows of dots are separated by the main color. In this example, it's 10 rows shown in white on the diagram. To make this stitch pattern interesting, the dots are alternated on the next row.

I've started by casting on and knitting 10 rows in the main color, ending with the carriage on the right. Remove the main yarn and put it aside. We'll pick it up again. The next steps will create a single row of knitting. Keep that in mind.

I plan to position the first dot five stitches from the edge, and then repeat dot units across the row with 11 stitches between each dot. So I'll count five plus seven needles, and then put the rest of the needles on the needle bed in hold.

Set the carriage to hold. Thread the carriage with the contrasting yarn. Knit across these 12 stitches and wrap. Now I want to concentrate on forming the dot. I'll put those first five needles in hold position and put two more needles in hold opposite the carriage.

There are five needles in work. Knit to the right and wrap. Notice I'm adding a claw weight in that dot section. Opposite the carriage, put two needles in hold and there are three needles in work. Knit across and wrap. Opposite the carriage, put one needle in hold.

There are two needles in work, knit across and wrap. That completes the dot. Let's look at working the next unit. We'll put the two held dot needles on the left into work. There should be four needles in work, plus put 11 needles for your spacer, plus seven needles for the next dot into working position.

So you'll have a total of 22 needles. The needles to the left are future dots and remain in hold. Still working with the contrasting yarn, knit across these 22 needles and wrap. The carriage will be on the left. Now, count seven needles in work next to the working yarn.

This is our new dot. We'll isolate that second dot by putting all needles but those seven into hold. Start forming the second dot by putting two needles opposite the carriage into hold. Knit across and wrap. Opposite the carriage, put two needles in hold.

Now there are three needles in work. Knit across and wrap. Opposite the carriage, put one needle in hold. And there are two needles left in work. Knit across and wrap. That finishes the second dot. Your carriage should be on the right.

Prepare for the third dot by putting needles into work as before following your diagram. Again, there should be a total of 22 needles in work. The needles to the left are future dots, and they remain in hold. Still working with the contrasting yarn, knit across these 22 needles and wrap.

When the last dot of this first row is complete, put all needles in hold position, cut the contrasting yarn, and free pass to pick up the main color yarn, and then knit 10 rows. We're ready to start the next dot row. Remove the main yarn from the feeder and set the carriage to hold.

We want the new dots to be positioned between the previous dots. According to my chart, I'll have 14 stitches plus 7 for the first unit. Put all needles except these 21 stitches in hold. Thread up the contrasting yarn and knit across these 21 stitches.

Now, identify the seven dot needles and put the others in hold, and then start forming your dot. Opposite the carriage, put two more needles in hold. There'll be five needles in work. Knit right and wrap. Opposite the carriage, put two more needles in hold.

There are three needles in work. Knit left and wrap. Opposite the carriage, put one needle in hold. There are now two needles in work. Knit right and wrap. As before, put two dot needles back into work, plus needles for the next unit.

Which is 11 plus 7. Knit across and wrap. Short row as before, forming the second dot. Continue working the units across the row to complete this second dot row. When the last dot is complete, cut the contrasting yarn, free pass to pick up the main color, and knit 10 rows.

Alternating the dots adds interest to your knitting. The best way to master the stitch pattern is to learn to do one unit and then think in terms of units across the row. It's best to work out your stitch pattern on graph paper.

Be sure to use odd numbers for the dots and odd numbers of needles for the stitches in between. One more thing to consider, you don't want to create bobbles by adding too many rows in the dots. This photo was taken before blocking, and you can see the raised dots.
So take care as to how many rows of the dots you're knitting for a single row of this stitch pattern.

A new knitter recently shared her goal sweater. She told me that the hand knitting pattern she wanted to use was a slip stitch pattern. But looking closely at the photo, it's a slip rib pattern incorporating both knit and purl stitches.

She has an LK150 knitting machine, so we offered her some options. The hand knitting stitch pattern is written row 1, knit 3, slip one purl-wise, row 2, purl across the row, and repeat these rows. We can translate this to machine knitting, keeping in mind that the purl stitches are always facing us on our knitting machine.

How about hand-manipulating every fourth stitch to create that slip rib? Here are two methods on a manual machine. First, knit about 10 rows and then manually drop every fourth stitch. When relatching each column of stitches, skip a row.

This will cause the stitch to elongate and produce this result. For the second method, I left every fourth needle out of work and then manually latched up the ladders, again skipping every other row, elongating in the knit stitch on that purl background.

Please try both of these methods to determine which one you prefer. Dropping and relatching the stitches created a looser and wider fabric. When keeping needles out of work, the strands forming the ladders are tighter, and the resulting fabric is also tighter and narrower.

If you have a ribber, you can make short work of this stitch pattern. Set up your needles like this, having every fourth needle on the main bed. This will create a three by one rib. Then set your main bed to slip in one direction.

This will form those elongated stitch columns automatically. This technique can also be worked on the ribber as Flat Rib. Keeping all needles in work on one bed and every fourth needle on the opposite bed, slipping every other row.
Slipped rib is a versatile technique that can have lots of uses. Try it with your machine and see which method you prefer.

When troubleshooting a knitting machine, the first question to ask is, how is your sponge bar? A flat sponge bar can be the culprit that causes a myriad of problems. It doesn't matter how old your machine is or how much it's been used, the sponge material deteriorates and it can no longer do the job of holding the needles in place.

On an LK150, it's often hard to determine if the sponge is flat. My machine was close to 10 years old, and I was really surprised at the condition of the sponge. The needles didn't seem to be loose, but the machine just wasn't knitting well.

Lesson learned: change your sponge bar before you start to struggle. Start by removing the carriage and the tension mast. Remove the clamps so you can turn the bed over. And remove each of your needles. Close the latch and pick up the by the needle butt and pull it back.

It should slip out pretty easily. For more details about removing and replacing needles, see the video at knititnow.Com/lk150needle. Once all the needles are out of the needle bed, you may want to take time to clean it. It's just plastic, so don't use any harsh chemicals or cleaners that might leave a residue.

Just a clean paint brush may be all you need. Turn the carriage over and remove the old sponge. Position the new sponge with the ribbon facing up. The needles will ride on this ribbon. We'll replace the needles by threading them over the sponge.

From the top of the bed, close the needle latch and push the hook down. use your fingers of your opposite hand to guide the hook down. Then push the back of the needle down to thread it over the sponge. Use your finger underneath to guide it back into the slot.

Do this for all 150 needles. Take it slow and don't be afraid of bending the needles. Use enough pressure to guide the needle down and over the sponge and then back up in the track towards the front of the bed. Replace each of the needles.

The LK150 originally had gray and pink rollers every 10 needles to help you keep track and position your knitting without having to count needles every time. Once you get a new sponge bar in place, you'll be amazed at how well your machine knits.

Sometimes when you're knitting, the edge stitches don't form properly. This could be caused by knitting too fast or taking the carriage out too far past the knitting, pulling that working yarn tight. If you find your carriage is jamming, watch for the formation of those edge stitches.
Notice the position of the needle butts and manually push them back, readjusting those misformed stitches.

Here are the steps for attaching the four color changer on a DM-80. The first thing to recognize is that the fasteners that attach both the extension plate and the color changer itself are in two parts. There's a threaded post and a threaded nut.

If you remove the nut, sometimes the threaded post will also be removed. Use a screwdriver to separate them. When installing the extension plate or the color changer, first insert and tighten the threaded post, then attach the threaded nut, leaving it loose enough to slip the attachments with their openings.

The extension and the color changer will be attached here. Then, tighten the nuts to secure the attachments. The four-color changer also requires this curved cam with three screws. the cam has three parts connected with those three screws.

Loosen the screws and attach the cam to the bed by inserting the round rod into the slot of the bed. Slide it to the left until it stops and then tighten the screws. When the four-color changer is installed, it fits snugly against that curved cam.

The two color yarn changer requires three parts the front bed extension, the two color changer, also called a feed box and the curved cam inserted in the back bed main rail. The first thing to recognize is that the fasteners that attach the extension plate are in two parts.

There's a threaded post and a threaded nut. If you remove the nut, sometimes the threaded post will also be removed. Use a screwdriver to separate them. First install the front bed extension with the threaded post and nut. If you already had a four color changer installed, remove the three part curved cam and replace it with the single bed curved cam underneath the bed.

Removed the threaded post and threaded nuts from the back bed. Slip the color changer over the posts that are in place in the bed and secure them with the wing nut. With this color changer, you'll be able to quickly change colors without having to rethread your machine each time.

Recently, more than a couple of knitters contacted me to tell me they just couldn't get their gauge right. One had knit a sleeve and it was way too long. The other one had knit an entire sweater and it was way too big. No, there isn't anything wrong with the pattern.

It's just math. Let's go back to the swatch and see where they're struggling. I often ask knitters to take a photo of their swatch with rulers. In a it doesn't matter if you use machine netter scale or a regular ruler. Often having another set of eyes to look at your swatch reveals the problem.

This knitter insisted that her gauge was 18.5 stitches to 4 inches. Now take a look and can you see that she had positioned her ruler scale along the edge of the knitting? The yellow ruler is designed to measure over 30 stitches.

Back to the drawing board, she measured between 30 stitches and got an accurate gauge. In this example, can you see the problem? Using the stitch scale to measure rows will cause all sorts of problems. Some time ago, a dear friend was sad because she had run out of yarn for her project.

She couldn't get any more of it. She showed me her swatch, and I was She was amazed. She told me the ball band said that the gauge was three stitches per inch, so she cast on three stitches and it measured one inch. What was wrong with that?

Obviously, she needed to knit a larger swatch. This last example has a whole bunch of problems. First, it isn't big enough. We need to knit a swatch that is large enough to measure a four-inch square in the middle. We can measure gauge more accurately without those curled edges impacting things.

Next, it looks like the knitter wants to use the yellow scale, but she needs 30 stitches in the middle of her knitting to use the scale. She didn't make a large enough swatch. Third, she marked some stitches with pins. But why take time to count stitches and do all that math?

Mark them as you knit and there's no counting. Next, the curled edges are going to make it much more difficult to measure accurately. Dress your swatch, wash, and block it as you're going to treat your project so that you can accurately measure.

It makes a big difference. Lastly, this bind-off edge is way too tight. It's distorting the edge, and the edge is making it impossible to measure the gauge accurately. I don't like to use the word worthless, but in this case, this knitter needs to start all over and knit a proper swatch that's large enough to mark stitches and rows according to the scale she'll use.
She needs to bind off loosely and dress her swatch. She'll have much more success with gauge in her knitting.

The edge springs are used to ensure that your edge stitches knit correctly. Although knitters say that they've successfully knit without using them, to prevent misformed stitches and possible jamming, it's best to get in the habit of positioning them while you're knitting.

The edge spring has a rounded ridge that fits into the rounded slot on the needle bed. The edge spring slips along the needle bed and is aligned with the outer edge needles the knitting. The latch of the edge needle must be closed.

The best way to ensure this is to position the edge spring. Push the latch needle out so the latch moves past the edge spring. Pull the needle back and the edge spring will close the latch automatically. Position the needle with the edge of the needle channel and you're ready to knit.

Here is a quick and easy full needle rib cast on that's just two rows. Now, before you try this, be sure you understand racking on your machine. Review this video if you need help. The instructions for this cast on start with rack H or swing H.

Pull up a few needles and confirm that your ribber is set to half pitch. The needles should be aligned like this. Now, because we'll be creating stitches on all needles, be sure to use a yarn that is finer than you might normally knit ribbing.

Set both beds for plain knitting. No tuck or slip buttons or levers are engaged. Set both carriages to the main tension for your garment or slightly tighter. Start by creating a zigzag row by knitting from right to left. Hang the cast-on comb, aligning it to the center and taking care not to split any stitches.

Hang weights as needed. Swing your ribber to the right so that the needles are aligned like this. No matter what machine you're using, make sure that the needles are not crashing into each other. Notice that the stitches are skewed to the right.

Knit one row to the right. Now, rack back to the left, and your needles should now be in the original position. Again, half pitch, and they're not crashing into each other. And continue knitting. Using the wire weight hangers can help.

The cast-on is complete, and this is called a full needle rib racked cast-on. This is a really fast cast-on, but it's fairly loose, and the cast-on comb can distort that first row. Don't try and tighten the first two rows of this cast-on.

The stitches need to be loose or large enough to rack. Consider casting on with waste yarn. Knit a few rows and then knit one row of ravel cord. Thread up the carriage with the main garment yarn and repeat that racked cast on over that ravel cord.
When you're done with your piece, you can remove the ravel cord and you've protected that cast on edge from the cast on comb.

Use this bind off anytime you're ending your knitting with needles out of work. You might be working a tuck lace pattern like this one with some needles out of work. Now, notice my needle arrangement. I have every third needle in work with two needles out of work.

Let's consider binding off in this needle arrangement. I'm using a 'round the gate peg method. I'll position my working yarn around the gate peg to the right of the stitch that I'm binding off. I'll pull the yarn through the stitch, keeping that extra loop around the gate peg.

Pull up a loop. Next, I'll position my latch tool in the empty space that was created from the needle out of work, and I'll just pull up a loop, creating a chain. Position the tool in the next space, keeping keeping the working yarn around that gate peg, and chain another loop.

Bind off the next stitch by putting it on the latch tool, grab the working yarn with the hook and pull it through the stitch. Keep that working yarn around the next gate peg, chain in the next space, and repeat for the second space, and then bind off the stitch.

Each time before you create a chain or bind off a stitch, position the working yarn around that gate peg for extra stretch. The bind off edge is worked around the gate pegs. When done, pop off those loops from the gate pegs and you'll have a beautiful, stretchy edge that accommodates the ladders that were created by the needles out of work.

Here is a beautiful ribber stitch pattern that was inspired by a hand knitting pattern called Textured Rib. It's basically 2x2 ribbing, slipping the knit stitches to highlight the purl stitches. More attractive than plain old 2x2 ribbing, it looks great on both sides.

I can't decide which side I like better. Instead of right and wrong side, I'm calling these side A and side B. The pattern is worked over a standard 2x2 needle set up. Two needles on the ribber, two needles on the main bed.

Then stitches are slipped every other row. I chose to slip on my ribber, keeping the main bed needles in work on every row. Of course, you could do it the opposite way, slipping on the main bed and knitting every row on the ribber.

Now, notice the slip strands on side B, adding interesting texture. I hope you'll give this stitch pattern a try. If you've struggled with 2x2 ribbing, the cast on can be a bit of a challenge at first. We have an entire course covering everything you need to know.
Knititnow. com/2x2 Happy Knitting.

Here's another ribber cast on that is stretchy, pretty, and easy to work. Similar to a single bed E-Wrap cast on, we're using it for 1x1 ribbing. Now you need some skills before you start this one. You need to have a basic 1x1 cast on of your choice.

You'll be casting on with waste yarn. You need to know how to set your machine for circular or tubular knitting. And understanding how to E-wrap helps. To make this cast on easier, start with scrap and ravel. Cast on in 1x1 ribbing in any method that you'd like, and hang your ribbon cast on comb.

Knit a few rows, and then end your scrap with a circular row of ravel cord. Knit across the main bed only with the ravel cord, then knit across the ribber only with ravel cord. Secure the ends of the ravel cord and end with the carriage on the right.

Change to your main yarn and e-wrap over all needles, alternating between the main bed needles and the ribber needles. Pulling the needles all the way out helps prevent mistakenly wrapping around the gate pegs. Wrap counterclockwise around the needles, trying to keep the wraps somewhat loose.

Thread up your carriage with your main yarn, set your desired tension, and knit across those E-wrapped stitches. That first row may be difficult to knit, but scrapping on makes this easier. The cast on comb and weights are in the scrap, not directly in the E-wraps.

Continue knitting and mark the side of the knitting that is facing you. Drop the work from the machine and examine the right and wrong sides of that cast-on edge. Notice that the side that was facing you has small purl bumps, but the cast-on edge that was away from you is neater.
The difference isn't too noticeable, but you might want to keep this in mind when you're planning your garment.

Circular knitting on the Titexma TH/TR 160 has one more step than some other machines. The secret to circular or tubular knitting on any machine is to understand the slip settings on each bed. The difference with this machine is that it only has one slip setting on the main bed.

With the carriage set in this position, the carriage will slip in both directions. On the ribber, you can choose to slip in only one direction. Get started in circular knitting on this machine with both beds set for plain knitting.

Cast on and knit full needle rib with all needles in work on both beds. Make sure the ribber is racked to "H" so the needles aren't crashing into each other, and knit a few rows. End with your carriage on the right. For the first row of circular knitting.

Leave the main bed carriage set for plain. The change lever will be set to plane and the side cam levers are set on "N". On the ribber, set it to slip left by putting the left side cam lever to print and make sure the tuck lever is set on "R".

In this example, the ribber will slip as you pass the carriage to the left. So knit across and only the main bed stitches will knit. Now, keeping those ribber settings the same throughout the whole piece, move the main bed change lever to "part", knit to the right.

Only the ribber needles will knit. You'll repeat rows 1 and 2 for circular knitting and you'll change the main bed setting every other row, keeping the ribber setting the same throughout. Row 1, your main bed carriage is set to plain.

You knit to the left and you'll knit the main bed only. Row 2, the main bed carriage is set to part and you'll knit to the right, and ribber stitches will knit only. So you'll change that main bed setting every other row from part to plane, part to plain every other row.
With circular knitting, you're alternating knitting on the ribber and knitting on the main bed, forming a tube.

Here is an oldie, but a goodie for finishing the edges of your knitting. It's not only pretty, it can also help tame the curl of plain stockinette knitting. Once you understand it and get a feeling for how it's worked, there are lots of variations to this trim that you can employ.

Working from right to left with the purl side of your knitting facing, use a three prong tool and hang the edge of the knitting on three needles. Set your carriage for plain knitting at a tension slightly tighter than your garment tension.

Knit four to six rows. You'll want to experiment with the tension for yourself. Moving along to the left, pick up the edge again with the three prong tool and hang the edge on those same three needles. Knit the same number of rows.

Keep picking up the edge stitches and hang them on those same three needles and knit the same number of rows. Continue in this manner until you reach a corner. At the corner, knit an extra two rows and then continue picking up the edge of the knitting.

In this example, we knit four rows between pickups and the texture isn't as defined. Experiment with your yarn. You can also fluff up the trim by picking up in this stitch, again. Pick up the edge, hang it on three needles, knit four to six rows, pick up the edge, hang it on the same needles, knit four to six rows, and continue all the way around the edge of your garment and you'll have a beautiful, worm trim.

Connecting DesignaKnit to your Brother electronic machine is a matter of connecting the BL1 or the BL5 cable between the machine and your computer with DAK installed. The USB cable has three parts. The USB end connects to a USB port on your computer.

The square end with the small prongs connects to the machine. On the 930, 940, remove the small plastic cover to reveal the port on the back of the machine. On the 970, the port is on the CB1 box. With the two ends now connected, the computer can now talk to the machine.

Next, position the black box, and I'm sure there's a better name for it, on the body of the machine near the row counter. Position it with the red dot facing the front of the machine and the cable tables towards the back.

Use Velcro to attach this so you can easily remove it to use it with other machines. Finally, position the Knitlink magnet arm to the K-carriage. Position it so it passes in front of the black box. On the 970, be sure that the arm clears the manual row counter.

As you pass the magnet, a red light will blink and a will be sent to DesignaKnit to record that you've passed the carriage and you've knit a row. You need to let DesignaKnit know what machine you're using and connect the computer to DesignaKnit.

I'm in Standard Garment Styling and from the menu, I'll choose >Options, click >Method of Knitting, then choose >Machine, and click >OK. Click the >Setup button and then click >Find Link and >start search. DesignaKnit will connect to your computer to set things up.

A message will display when the connection is made. Click >OK. Scroll to choose your machine and then click >OK. With everything in place, your machine and DesignaKnit will be able to talk to each other. In interactive Knitting, the magnet will let DesignaKnit know you've knit a row, and DesignaKnit will give you your knitting instructions.

In Stitch Designer, this setup will allow you to download stitch patterns to your machine or upload built-in stitch patterns to DesignaKnit so that you can modify them. If you'd like to learn more about using DesignaKnit , please visit learnDesignaKnit.
Com.

Follow along as I knit one side of my baby cardigan using a knit radar. Shape your knitting by following along the lines. My gauge is 28 stitches to 4 inches, and I'm using the appropriate stitch scale. On the mylar, the drawing is aligned to the left at the zero mark of the stitch scale.

To get started, the instruction is cast on 30 stitches. The numbers and the tick marks on the scale represent the needles on the needle bed. We'll cast on needles, right 1 to right 30, and then I'll continue knitting without any shaping until I get to the arm hole shaping.

At this point, I'm reading that I need to bind off, decrease, or short row three stitches. Notice that the line is between the three and four marks on the scale. Now, this is not an exact science, so I'll use my judgment and choose to bind off three stitches and make notes as I go.

Because I'm going to be duplicating this shaping while knitting the other cardigan front, I'll note my shaping right on the mylar as I knit. After knitting two rows, the curved arm hole line is indicating that I need to bind off, short row or decrease two more stitches.

The tick mark is indicating right needle number five. Knitting two more rows, I'll decrease one stitch, right needle number six. Knitting two more rows, decrease one stitch, right needle number seven. Now you can use whatever shaping methods you'd like decreasing bind off or short rows.

This is just giving you the numbers to use. We've decreased a total of eight stitches. Following the straight section of that arm hole opening, I'll continue to knit to row 57 until I see this neckline shaping. Now remember to document your shaping as you work.

This time I'm going to decrease one stitch on the right side. I'll knit two rows, decrease two stitches, knit two rows, decrease or short row five stitches, knit two rows, decrease two, knit two rows, and decrease two. I'm choosing to do my shaping every other row.

You can choose to do your shaping in other intervals if you'd like. Just follow the lines so you get the shaping that you drew on your mylar. As my neck opening shaping is complete, there will be stitches on needle right nine through right 19.

Knit over these 10 stitches for the shoulders and then bind off or scrap off on row 68. This completes one side of my cardigan. Now to knit the other side of the cardigan, we'll reverse the shaping. We'll cast on left 1 through left 30.

Instead of shaping the arm hole on the left, we're going to shape the arm hole on the right, following the lines and the needle numbers. Then we'll shape the neck line on the opposite edge of the arm hole shaping. If this is confusing for you, draw a left and right side on your mylar, but remember to duplicate the shaping instructions so both sides match.

Keeping track of the stitch counts for our cardigan fronts was pretty straightforward. If we were knitting for an adult, even at one-half scale, the sleeve probably really won't fit on the mylar. So we'll just draw half of the sleeve and half of the sweater back.

As we're knitting, we'll still follow the lines, but we'll mirror the shaping on both sides of the needle bed. For example, on this sleeve, I'll cast on 40 stitches, needles right 20 and left 20. The shaping is mirrored on each side of zero.

Add waist shaping to any sweater with a little math and the Knit It Now Magic formula tools. This summer sweater has no waist shaping. A fellow knitter, Sandy, decided she wanted to shape her sweater by removing a total of eight inches, four inches from the front and four inches from the back.

We'll create shaping instructions in two steps. First, after the one-inch hem, we'll start to decrease for five inches to the waist. For a better fit and drape, we'll knit one inch without any shaping at the waist. Then we'll immediately increase for five inches back up to the bust width.

The goal is to decrease gradually from hip to waist and then increase back waist to bust. We'll use the Knit It Now Magic Formula tool for this. Go to Patterns, Charting Tools. Since we know our dimensions, we'll use the Magic Formula tool in inches or centimeters.

We will be shaping both sides of the piece, her gage at 28 and 38. The starting width at the hem is 18 inches and the waist is going to be 14 inches. The height of this section is 5 inches. Now be sure to let the tool know if you're working in inches or centimeters.

And click Create your Knitting Instructions. Here are her knitting instructions. Draw her on and out, you can see that there's a nice smooth line for her sweater. We'll do the same thing for the upper part of this waist shaping.

Again, using the tool for both sides, I'll enter her gage, then the starting and ending width and height. She will insert these instructions when knitting the body of her sweater. With the tool, there's no complicated math.
Just determine the measurements you want and create your custom knitting instructions.

We're going to be working over half of the stitches on the needle bed. Start by determining which needle is going to be used as the center, and mark the needle bed with a pencil. This mark can be easily erased and will help you keep track as you're transferring stitches, especially if you're transferring groups of stitches across the row.

You'll see in a minute that I didn't remember this trick until I knit my second set of transfers. Cast on stitches as instructed and make the first decrease, emptying a needle. Then hang a transfer tool on those first couple of left-hand needles for safety so they won't fall off in the next step.

Pull out all of the needles on the right Slip those stitches to the garter bar, and try to open the latches as you remove the stitches. This isn't critical. You can always open latches, but it helps if you do it with the garter bar.

Transfer the stitches left. When you rehang the stitches from the garter bar, you'll be filling in that empty needle, and you'll have one last stitch on the right finishing your decrease. Don't forget to remove that safety transfer tool.

Take that emptied needle out of work before you continue knitting, and knit two rows. Repeat this process, making sure you work your decreases over the same needle each time. Done correctly, you'll have shaped your piece with the decreases and have a decorative seam.

The first thing you might do with a garter bar is to remove stitches from the machine and rehang them. I've knit a bit of stockinette with weight. Having weight on the knitting is important. I've pulled the needles all the way out and make sure all the latches are open.

Position the garter bar over the needles. The hooks of the needles will go in the slots. Gently pull the stitches off the needles onto the bar. As you pull the stitches, the latches will close and that stitch will slip right onto the garter bar.

Now, you'll be nervous the first time you do this, but with practice, it gets easier. Push the stitches all the way to the back of the bar, and then tilt the bar up, releasing it from the hooks, and remove the knitting from the machine.

At this point, you could set the work aside or move the entire piece, working increases and decreases, returning the stitches to the needles. To rehang the stitches, make sure the latches are open and put the slots of the bar in the hooks of the needles again.

Slide the stitches back onto the needles. If you have a needle stopper, it can secure the needles and make it easier to rehang the stitches. The second way you can use a garter bar is to remove the knitting from the machine, turn it around, rehang the stitches, and knit a row.

Adding purl stitches. Although it's not practical to knit the equivalent of garter stitch this way, but just for a few rows, this could be a real time saver over scrapping off or manually reforming stitches. Unlike the vintage style of garter bar that has hills and valleys, the KhrisKrafter's style is much more straightforward.

Let's explore RTR, remove, turn, and rehang with this style of garter bar. I have a bit of knitting on the machine and I want to add a garter ridge, maybe for an accent or a turning row. I have weight on the knitting. Now, this is important.

I'll stop knitting with the carriage on the right. First, I like to remove the working yarn from the yarn feeder of the carriage. Now, if you forget to do this, no problem. I just like to make it a habit. I'll position the garter bar over the needles, putting the hooks in the slots of the bar.

Notice that the perl side or the wrong or the private side of the knitting is facing me right now. I'll slip the stitches to the bar and push them all the way to the back of the bar. As you remove the stitches, use the bar to open the latches.

Once your knitting is off the machine, pass your carriage to the opposite side of the needle bed so the working yarn is in position to knit. Again, confirm that all the latches are open. With the stitches pushed to the back of the bar, before you turn and rehang the work, hook, notice that there are little openings.

We'll insert the hooks of the needles in these openings to rehang the stitches. Now, turn the bar and your knitting so the knit side is facing. To rehang the stitches, lay the bar flat, positioning the hooks in those openings.

Rotate the bar down and you can see that the hooks are catching the stitches. If a latch is closed, it's going to prevent the hooks from picking up that stitch. Pull down to slip the garter bar out of the stitches and remove it completely.

Check to see if any stitches have split or are not in the hooks, and use a transfer tool to manually repair them. Next, push the work back and knit a row. Notice the purl bumps facing you. To complete a garter row, we'll repeat the steps and turn the work again.

Remove the knitting from the machine, turn the bar and the knitting, and re-hang it on the machine. This time, when I re-hung my work, I remembered to use the needle stopper. If you have one, it can be really helpful. Once the stitches are back on the machine, knit a few rows and admire your single garter ridge.

No matter what knitting patterns you use, adjusting the length of your sleeves isn't difficult. Use the Knit It Now Magic formula tool and let us do the math for you. I want to make my sleeve three inches shorter than the pattern.

The original pattern length is 16.75 inches plus 2 inches for ribbing. I'm going to keep my wrist measurement the same at nine inches, and I'm going to keep the upper arm measurement the same at 14.5. All I want to adjust is the sleeve length.

I'll make it 13.75 and keep the ribbing at 2 inches. I'll use the Magic Formula tool in inches. Now, the shaping is going to be for both sides of my sleeve. I'll enter my gauge. The starting width is the wrist measurement of 9 inches and the ending width is the upper arm measurement of 14.5 inches.
I want the shaped section of my sleeve to be 13.75. Here are my knitting instructions. All of the increases are evenly spaced and my sleeve will be the perfect length.

Another use of the latch tool is for binding off. Knit the last row of your knitting at the loosest tension, or manually knit a loose row. Slip the first stitch off the needle and place it on the tool, behind the latch of the tool.

Slip the adjacent stitch to the tool in the hook on the tool. Pull the second stitch through the first. This is called a stitch-through stitch bind off. Method is fast, but it may not be as stretchy as you need. Please try other bind-off methods in addition to this one.

The latch tool is most commonly used to reverse stitches, turning knit stitches into purl stitches. Notice how the purl bump is showing against the knit stitches in this example. To reform an existing stitch, push the tool into a stitch below the one that's currently in work on a needle.

Drop the stitch off the needle and ravel it, forming a ladder. Use the tool to pick up each ladder, forming new stitches. To create a column of reformed stitches, drop a single stitch, pick up each ladder, forming new stitches.

When the last strand has been knit, rehang the stitch on the needle. Now you have a column of reformed stitches. This can be done across a row for a turning row or a manually formed decorative purl row. Anytime you use a latch tool, remember, you're positioning a needle in the opposite direction of the needles on the needle bed.
If you reform stitches, they will be facing the opposite way. Think about knit and purl stitches as in hand knitting.

Using traveling stitches to frame eyelets can create a beautiful, decorative stitch pattern for your knitting. As machine knitters, because the purl side faces us as we knit, this can be a bit confusing at first. This is one of those techniques that you have to try it to get it.

The secret is to get a mental picture of the effect from the knit side or the finished side of the work. To make the stitches travel, we'll work a two-step transfer. First, we'll identify the traveling stitch. Then transfer the stitch next to it, doubling up the stitches.

Then move both stitches to fill that emptied needle. This transfer empties the eyelet needle. Make sure you keep that eyelet needle in work and knit two rows. Next, identify that traveling stitch again by following your chart, and you can also reach underneath and feel the bulk of that traveling stitch.

Transfer the stitch next to it, doubling up the stitches and emptying a needle. Take both of those stitches and transfer them to fill the emptied needle. Moving these two stitches empties the eyelet needle. Make sure that that eyelet needle remains in work and knit two rows.

You'll continue this for the stitch pattern. Now, you can also keep track of the traveling stitch by needle number by creating a chart. Use Knitter's Graph paper and draw out what you want your traveling stitches to look like.

Your best bet is to try this on a swatch. Once you take it off the machine, the light bulb will come on and you can get creative with positioning traveling eyelets across your knitting. Don't forget that these eyelets are going to impact your stitch and row gauge, so be sure to swatch in pattern.

My swatch has given me so much information that I can now use to plan my hand knit blanket. Nope, I'm not knitting this one on the machine. First, I don't have enough needles and I don't want to knit panels. Next, this is going to be a get-out- of-the-studio project just for fun.

But the planning would be the same if I was going to knit this on the machine. I want my like it to be 50 inches wide and 72 inches long. At my gauge, that means I need to knit 250 stitches for 72 inches. When hand knitting, we don't have to count rows like in machine knitting.

And honestly, I'll probably knit until I run out of yarn. Speaking of running out of yarn, my swatch is 6 inches by 7.5 inches and it weighs 18 grams. I used the Knit It Now yarn estimator and entered 6 by 7.5 and 18 grams.

To knit this blanket, 50 inches by 72 inches, I'll need about 1440 grams. My yarn comes in 100-gram balls, so the 15 that I bought will be just right. I'm planning a garter stitch border. My swatch reminded me that the garter stitch gauge is considerably wider and shorter than my stitch pattern.

Can you see how the edge dips on this side? I just plan to block this out so it isn't so noticeable. This is just a blanket after all. But the top and bottom borders are really flaring out. I've charted my 50-inch wide blanket based on my stitch pattern gauge.

To prevent the garter edges from flaring out, I'll cast on about 10% fewer stitches. I'll knit the border, and then I'll increase back up to the required 250 stitches and continue to knit my blanket in pattern. When I get to within about two inches of the finished length, I'll decrease evenly across the row and then finish the border in garter stitch over 225 stitches.

By changing the stitch count, I'll prevent this. I'm kind of embarrassed to share this, but as a new knitter many, many moons ago, I didn't understand the relationship between the seed stitch border and the beautiful cable panels of this project.
