Although this is a treasured family heirloom, I cringe every time I use this blanket. Now, as I've been working with this stitch pattern by hand, I realized that we could knit this on the machine. It's basically, a three by three rib set up with the ribber.

Knit two rows, transfer stitches between the beds, knit two rows, and continue. For a smaller project, all those transfers might not be too bad. But that's for another day. I need to get away from the studio and get knitting on this promised blanket for my granddaughter.

Knitting cables on the knitting machine can be a challenge. The crossing of the stitches can be difficult, plus adding purl stitches for a hand knit look can be tedious. Now, I've always considered using the ribber to add purl stitches, but I'd never tried it.

Here are the results of my experiment with this idea. I set up my knitting with four needles in work on the main bed and two needles in work on the ribber. I'm planning a two by two cable with two purl stitches between each cable.

Remember that when we're crossing cables on the machine, we're stretching those stitches considerably, relying on the stretch of the yarn to make the cross. You may even notice that my needles are being pulled out of position.

And this is just a simple two by two cable. Nothing fancy. What I found is that no matter how I held the transfer tools, no matter what angle I held them, this is clumsy at best. Plus, the stitches on the ribber are very tight and tend to pop off and misform.

Try it yourself, but I'll bet you have similar results. My conclusion with this experiment is that I'll cross cables on the single bed and relatch purl stitches that I want. Or, better yet, leave cables for hand knitting projects.
What do you think?

Here's a cast on that may not be the prettiest, but it's closed and fast. This is a Silver Reed 860 mid gauge machine, and the setup would be similar to other Singer / Studio / Silver Reed machines. The cast on uses slip stitch.

Slip settings on the machine means needles in working or B position do not knit and the yarn passes under those needles. Let's get started by pulling a few needles all the way out. With the carriage set for plain knitting, the cam lever is on O, the side levers are on the triangle, pass the carriage a couple of times and align the needles into B position.

End with the carriage on the right. With your needle pusher, pull every other needle to hold position or D or all the way out, keeping those alternate needles in B position. Set the carriage to slip by engaging both the side levers to the circle position and set the cam lever to slip.

Thread your carriage and knit to the left. Secure that tail with a clip or a close pin. Notice how there are loops over every other needle, and the needles that were in B position do not have loops. Now, this may seem a bit counterintuitive, but that's the way slip works.

With your carriage on the left, pull the empty needles all the way out, knit across, and notice that these needles now also have loops. Do this one more time. Pull those first same set of needles and knit left. Then pull the alternate needles and knit right.

Cancel slip by setting both side levers to the triangle and the cam lever to O for plain knitting. Knit a few rows and take a look at the edge. Not too pretty, but it is stable and fast, and it works great for scraping on.

These quick fingerless mitts offer endless possibilities for being creative. I knit this pair about 10 times in my mind, considering all the different variations I could use. Thankfully, I still have lots of yarn and can make another pair using more of the ideas I've been considering.

Here's what I ended up deciding. I knit a long piece of ribbing. The entire arm is in one by one ribbon, and it fits nice and snug. The hand is plain stockinette. I finished it with about one inch of ribbing, and instead of messing with binding off that ribbing, I knit a few plain rows and bound off.

This rolled edge saved me from a tedious Kitchener stitch bind-off, and it's a nice decorative touch. If you aren't familiar with this cast-on, it just adds a strand in the tubular edge that I can pull up. I gathered up this edge and hit it with a shot of steam to set it.

This keeps the cast on edge from flaring out. Following my pattern, I knit in ribbing to the start of the thumb opening, and then I placed markers on each side. I was done with my ribbing, so I transferred all of the stitches to the main bed.

I knit to the end of the thumb opening and placed another set of markers. Now this is designed as a fast project, so there isn't a thumb and no messing around with the thumb gore. Again, following my pattern, I finished the hand in stockinette.

I transferred the stitches back down to the ribber, switched out the connecting arm, and raised my ribber. I knit one inch in ribbing. Now, one more time, I transferred the stitches back to the main bed and dropped the ribber, switching the connecting arms and just knit a few rows.

Binding off loosely here will allow my mitten to stretch over my fingers, but the one inch of ribbing will keep it snug. Seaming with this yarn that has very little twist was a bit of a challenge. It wanted to fray and break.

I was reminded of a suggestion years ago from a very experienced knitter that I could use a different yarn for my seam, something that doesn't fray or break. Done neatly, no one will ever know that I used a different yarn to seam.
With all this yarn left, I can't wait to start another pair. They're so soft and comfy and nice and warm for this cold weather here in Southern California.

There are two options for transferring stitches from the ribber to the main bed. You can also use this the other way. From the main bed down to the ribber using a double eyed needle. First take the stitch off onto that double eyed needle.

Flip the needle and slide the stitch to the other end. Then position the opening of the double eyed needle over the hook of the main bed needle and slip off the stitch. Now this looks harder than it is. Once you get a feel for it and establish a rhythm, it goes pretty quickly.

If you're like me and your double eyed needle likes to play hide and seek, try using two transfer tools. From the top, slip the ribber stitch to the transfer tool and put the ribber needle out of work. From the bottom, insert a second transfer tool into the stitch and transfer that stitch to the new tool.

Put the eye of that second tool over the main bed needle and slip the stitch to the main bed needle. Again, this looks harder than it is and you may prefer this method even if you can find that pesky double eyed needle.

Now watch your yarn. It takes at least three times the width of the working yarn to knit one row. I noticed I was running low, so I unthreaded the yarn and laid it across the needle bed. It didn't quite measure three times, so I'm going to cut the yarn and start a new ball.

To work in that first yarn tail, I pulled out a few needles and ran the tail over and under those needles. I threaded up the new ball of yarn, leave a tail of the new ball, and knit across the row, securing the first tail.

You can safely cut that first tail now. Before you knit back, wrap the new tail over and under the opposite needles at the beginning of that row. Knit across and secure that second tail. And at any time, it's safe to cut that second tail.

Continue knitting, watching your row counter. This is a neat and tidy way to secure yarn tails when knitting stripes or adding a new ball of yarn without having to work them in when you're done knitting.

I'm working a broken toe cast on to end up with a nice tubular edge for my ribbing. My needles are arranged for one by one ribbing, and I'll start with a zigzag cast on. Both carriages are set for plain knitting. I'll hang the ribber cast on comb, making sure the comb is hanging in the loops of the ribber needles.

Next, I'll disengage the ribber carriage the carriage from the main carriage, pass it, and drop all the ribber loops. The cast on comb will be hanging in those loops. I'll pass the carriage back and rejoin the ribber and the main bed carriages.

There are no changes to the carriages yet. I'll knit another zigzag row. Notice that the main bed now has stitches and the ribber now has new loops. At this point, I'll hang weights in my cast on comb. Next, I'll knit the tubular rows with slip.

I'll set the main bed to slip in one direction and the ribber to slip in the opposite direction. In other words, I'm going to knit only the ribber stitches first, then knit only the main bed stitches, then knit only the ribber stitches.

I'll finish by canceling slip on both carriages and set for plain knitting, and then knit one row in ribbing. Following my pattern, I'll continue knitting in ribbing. When the ribbing rows are complete, I'll transfer the ribber stitches to the main bed.
